itineraries.title: Algarve in 7 Days: Ria Formosa, Benagil, Lagos, and Sagres
itineraries.subtitle: Explore the Algarve in 7 days, based first in Tavira and then in Lagos, from the islands of Ria Formosa to the cliffs of Sagres.
itineraries.notes: Since August 2024, landing on the beach inside Benagil Cave has no longer been allowed; the cave can only be viewed from a boat or a guided kayak. From October through March, public ferries to the Ria Formosa islands are infrequent: check the schedules at the Olhão dock the day before.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with highs of 23 to 27 °C in Faro and sea temperatures around 22 to 24 °C in September. Avoid July and August if possible: afternoon temperatures exceed 29 °C, and boats, beaches, and trails are crowded. November and December are the rainiest months, with 75 to 90 mm of rain per month.
specialties: Lagune et îles de la Ria Formosa
Héritage musulman et des Grandes Découvertes

visits.text: Bills clatter overhead as storks nest atop the Arco da Vila, the main gateway to the Cidade Velha, Faro’s old town. Bishop Francisco Gomes do Avelar commissioned this arch from Italian architect Francisco Xavier Fabri. It was inaugurated in 1812. Once you have walked through, turn around: behind the facade is a much older gateway, a horseshoe arch from the Muslim period, probably dating to the 11th century.

The best view of Ria Formosa, the lagoon fringed by sandy islands along Faro’s coast, takes some effort: about 68 steps lead to the top of the tower of the Sé, the cathedral. Construction began in 1251, two years after the Christian reconquest of the city. In 1596, English troops under the Earl of Essex looted and burned it. Admission costs €5. Visit on a weekday: on Sundays, the church is generally reserved for services.

Discovered in 1926 beneath two streets in Faro, a Roman mosaic of Oceanus, the sea deity, is the highlight of the Museu Municipal de Faro. It is classified as a national treasure. The museum occupies the Convent of Nossa Senhora da Assunção, where construction began in 1519. Its cloister, completed in 1548, is one of Portugal’s earliest Renaissance-style cloisters. The convent is also in the old town: combine your visit with the Sé.

“Stop here and consider that you too will reach this state”: the inscription above the entrance to the Capela dos Ossos, the Chapel of Bones, sets the tone. Opened in 1816 behind the Igreja do Carmo, it is lined with the bones of more than a thousand Carmelite monks, including 1,245 skulls. The room measures just 4 m by 6 m. Visit on a weekday: on Saturdays, it is only open in the morning.

map_keywords: Centro de Educação Ambiental de Marim

visits.text: Two matching red-brick market halls stand on the waterfront: these are the Mercados de Olhão, built in the early 20th century. One sells fish, the other fruit, vegetables, and cheese. A replica of the Bom Sucesso, a small sailing vessel, is moored nearby. In 1808, Olhão rose up against the French occupation. Seventeen men then sailed aboard it to Brazil, where the Portuguese court had taken refuge, to deliver the news. Arrive between 7:30 and 9 a.m. to see the morning catch.

Climb the bell tower of the Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora do Rosário, a 17th-century Baroque church built by fishermen: from above, Olhão looks like a set of white building blocks. These houses in the Bairro da Barreta, the oldest fishing neighborhood, have flat rooftop terraces known as açoteias. Families watched for returning boats, dried fish, and slept there in summer. This style is linked to historic exchanges with North Africa. There is a small fee to climb the bell tower.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip in Ria Formosa, choose Ilha da Culatra. Ria Formosa is a natural park spanning 60 km of coastline, with five sandy islands forming a barrier against the ocean. Culatra is about 6 km long, has no cars, and is home to some 700 residents. At its western tip, the 46 m Santa Maria lighthouse offers free visits on Wednesdays from 2 to 5 p.m. The public ferry leaves from the dock beside the market halls: 30 minutes to Culatra, 45 minutes to Farol, the lighthouse hamlet.

practical_info.tip: A one-way ticket costs €2.10 to Culatra and €2.40 to Farol. In summer, more than ten boats depart each day; in winter, there are only a few, and schedules change every month. Before leaving, note the last return departure time at the ticket counter.

activities.text: Less well known than the islands, the Centro de Educação Ambiental de Marim, the natural park’s discovery center, deserves two hours of your time. It is about 3 km east of Olhão. A 3 km loop trail passes a tide mill, which ran on seawater held back at high tide and released at low tide. It also passes Roman fish-salting tanks and bird-watching blinds. Look out for the western swamphen, a large blue-purple bird with a red bill. Admission costs €3.20.

practical_info.tip: Bring binoculars and visit early in the morning or late in the day, when birds are most active.

visits.text: It is called the Ponte Romana, the “Roman bridge,” yet an archaeological study showed that the Romans did not build it. This seven-arch bridge connects the two banks of the Gilão, the river that divides Tavira in two. In 1989, a flood swept away two of its arches, and it was restored in 1992. Walk across it from Praça da República late in the day, when the facades are reflected in the water.

The Castelo de Tavira, built by the Moors, crowns the hill in the old town. Its ramparts offer views across all the rooftops. Right beside it, the Igreja de Santa Maria do Castelo was built in the 13th century on the ruins of a mosque, and its bell tower was rebuilt using the former minaret. It houses the tomb of Dom Paio Peres Correia, the Christian commander who retook the town from the Moors in 1242. His seven knights, killed during a truce, lie nearby. Church admission costs €4, including the climb up the bell tower.

In 1551, Tavira gained the Igreja da Misericórdia, whose Renaissance doorway is framed by columns and topped by Our Lady of Mercy. Inside, panels of azulejos, painted glazed ceramic tiles, have covered the walls since the 18th century. Tavira has 37 churches, but this one is on the climb up to the castle: stop in along the way.

A terracotta vessel with small human and animal figures lining its rim: this is the Vaso de Tavira, the star exhibit at the Núcleo Museológico Islâmico. This small museum is built around remains from the Muslim period. You can see a 12th-century rampart made of rammed earth, meaning soil compacted in layers inside formwork. Ask at the front desk for the translated visitor booklet to help you follow the exhibits.

If the sky is clear, head up the Torre de Tavira, the former water tower built in 1931. Slated for demolition, it was saved by local residents, who voted to preserve it in a referendum on June 13, 1999. At a height of 30 m, a camera obscura, a kind of periscope made of mirrors and lenses, projects a live image of the town onto a screen. The demonstration lasts about 20 minutes and takes place on weekdays from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

activities.text: Park at Pedras d’El Rei, cross the footbridge over the lagoon, then board the little train that travels 1.3 km through the dunes to Praia do Barril. On the sand, 203 rusty anchors form the Cemitério das Âncoras, the Anchor Cemetery. They held the nets of the almadrava, a maze of nets used to trap tuna, on the seabed. The fishermen left them there in 1964, when the fishing camp was abandoned. Their former huts now house cafés.

practical_info.tip: The little train costs €2 one way and €4 round trip. You can also walk the 1.3 km along the path beside the tracks.

activities.text: If you like octopus, have lunch in Santa Luzia, a fishing village west of Tavira. It is nicknamed the “octopus capital,” and its restaurants have made octopus their specialty. The village is on the road to Pedras d'El Rei: stop on your way to or from Praia do Barril.

practical_info.tip: In summer, reserve a table, especially on weekends.

visits.text: The Michelin Guide ranks Praia da Marinha among Europe's ten most beautiful beaches, and the view from the clifftop makes it easy to see why. The sandy beach is framed by orange limestone cliffs that the sea has carved into rock formations. It is near the hamlet of Caramujeira, in the municipality of Lagoa. The path down to the beach is steep: keep your closed-toe shoes on and take in the panorama from above first.

activities.text: Since August 2024, new rules have governed visits to Algar de Benagil, a sea cave with a large round opening in its roof. Between Lagos and Albufeira, it is the only cave carved by the sea from both the side and above: the ceiling collapsed, letting sunlight in. Landing on its interior beach or swimming into the cave is now prohibited. Kayaks may enter only with a guide, and each boat stays inside for just a few minutes.

practical_info.tip: Fishing boats depart from Benagil Beach. In summer, book an early morning trip to avoid the wait.

activities.text: Wear sturdy shoes for the Percurso dos Sete Vales Suspensos, the Seven Hanging Valleys Trail: 5.7 km along the cliffs between Praia da Marinha and Praia de Vale Centeanes. These small valleys end abruptly at the cliff edge, overlooking the sea. The trail passes above Benagil and Praia do Carvalho, then ends near Alfanzina Lighthouse. Stay well back from the edge and the algares, natural shafts carved into the limestone by water.

practical_info.tip: There is almost no shade: set out early in the morning or late in the afternoon, and bring water. The trail is linear: return the same way or take a taxi.

visits.text: Golden-yellow rock pillars, some reaching 20 m high, rise from the sea below Ponta da Piedade Lighthouse, which dates to 1913. The headland is about 3 km from central Lagos, a 40-minute walk along the coast. A staircase with more than a hundred steps leads down to the water. Come early in the morning or at sunset: in summer, the free parking lot is full between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Behind its plain facade, Igreja de Santo António hides an interior covered in carved, gilded woodwork known as talha dourada. Damaged in the 1755 earthquake, the church was restored in 1769, when its blue-and-white azulejos and dome were installed. Six paintings depict the miracles of Saint Anthony. Entry is through Museu Dr. José Formosinho, open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. Admission costs €3, or €5 including the slavery museum.

In 1444, a Portuguese expedition sold 235 African captives in the square where the Mercado de Escravos de Lagos now stands. They were the first African slaves sold in Europe in the modern era. Henry the Navigator, who financed the expedition, received one-fifth of their value. The current building, dating to 1691, houses the Rota da Escravatura museum, the route of slavery. The visit is brief and sober: allow 45 minutes.

To understand Lagos, follow its 16th-century ramparts from Praça do Infante, where the statue of Henry the Navigator stands. In the 15th century, the city was the center of Portuguese maritime exploration, and Henry lived here most of the time. Gil Eanes, a sailor from Lagos, was the first to sail past Cape Bojador on the African coast, in 1434. Allow 30 minutes for a walk along the ramparts.

Head down to Praia Dona Ana, a sandy cove surrounded by rocks sculpted by the sea. At high tide, the cliffs divide it into several small coves. A little farther toward Ponta da Piedade, a wooden staircase leads to Praia do Camilo. Come at low tide to walk from one cove to another.

activities.text: If the sea is calm, take a boat tour of the Ponta da Piedade caves from Lagos. Allow 60 to 90 minutes and €25 to €40 per person, depending on the boat and trip length. Boats enter several of the caves carved into the cliffs. For a quieter outing, guided kayak or paddleboard trips depart from Praia da Batata year-round, costing around €35 to €50.

practical_info.tip: Book the day before in summer and choose a day with calm seas: swells rock the small boats.

visits.text: Henry the Navigator is said to have founded a navigation school here, but there is no evidence to support the story. Fortaleza de Sagres, on a clifftop plateau at the end of the headland, was indeed built in the 15th century on his orders. Henry died in Sagres in 1460. On the ground, the Rosa dos Ventos (compass rose), a large stone circle divided into 32 directions, may have served as a sundial. Admission has cost €10 since 2025: afterward, walk around the headland with a windbreaker on.

The wind blows hard, and the cliffs plunge 75 m straight into the Atlantic: at Cape St. Vincent, you are at the southwestern tip of mainland Europe. The Romans called it the sacred promontory. The lighthouse, built in 1846 on the ruins of a convent, casts its beam 60 km out to sea. The lighthouse tower is currently closed to visitors indefinitely. For sunset, arrive an hour early. Touristy but fun: a truck here sells a sausage billed as “the last one before America.”

Fortaleza do Beliche, a small fort between Sagres and the cape, once protected tuna fishermen from pirates. It dates to the reign of Manuel I or John III in the 16th century, and the English privateer Francis Drake attacked it in 1587. Its Santa Catarina chapel, which partly overhangs the cliff edge, is closed to visitors because of the risk of collapse. Below lies Praia do Beliche, a sandy beach between the cliffs: stop on your way to the cape.

activities.text: Board a boat at Porto da Baleeira, Sagres's fishing harbor, for a dolphin-watching trip. Trips aboard rigid inflatable boats last about 1 hour 30 minutes and run year-round, starting at around €40 per adult. Choose an operator with marine biologists on its team: they explain what you see. The water stays cool, from 15 °C in winter to 19 °C in summer, and the wind makes it feel even cooler out at sea.

practical_info.tip: Dress warmly, even in summer, and bring something to protect your phone from sea spray.

activities.text: Depending on the wind, Sagres offers a calm beach or a beach for surfers. South-facing Praia da Mareta, a few minutes' walk from town, is the most sheltered. Southeast-facing Praia do Martinhal suits families, with lifeguards in summer. West-facing Praia do Tonel gets the biggest waves and strongest currents: leave it to experienced surfers.

practical_info.tip: Keep a wetsuit on if you want to swim for a long time: the water barely exceeds 19 °C, even in August.

visits.text: At 902 m, Fóia is the highest point in the Algarve, in the Serra de Monchique. The summit bristles with antennas and an air force radar station: the setting is hardly pristine, but on a clear day the view stretches to the Atlantic. Choose a cloudless day, or all you will see is fog.

Walk up through the narrow streets of Monchique to the Igreja Matriz, the town’s main church, dating from the 16th century. Its portal is Manueline, the Portuguese decorative style from the reign of King Manuel I. Here, it is carved with motifs drawn from nature. Inside, you will see 18th-century azulejos and a Baroque altarpiece, a large carved decorative structure behind the altar.

Water emerges from the ground at 32 °C in Caldas de Monchique, a small spa village about 6 km south of the town. These springs have been renowned for their beneficial properties since Roman times, and Portugal’s royal family used to spend the season here. Stop for a break on your way down to Silves.

activities.text: Medronho is the Serra de Monchique’s fruit brandy, distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, a shrub with small red berries. Try a small glass at a café in town. It is a strong spirit: if you are driving, limit yourself to a drop or take a bottle home.

practical_info.tip: Try the honey from the serra, too: it is used in most local cakes and desserts.

visits.text: The red ramparts of Castelo de Silves are visible from afar at the top of the town. Their color comes from Silves sandstone, a reddish local stone. The 11th-century Muslim fortress covers about 12,000 m² and has eleven towers. In 1189, King Sancho I captured it with the help of crusaders on their way to the Holy Land. The Almohad army from North Africa recaptured it as early as 1191. Head down to see the Cisterna da Moura, a water reservoir 10 m high. Admission costs less than €4.

Just below the castle, Sé de Silves, a former cathedral, is one of southern Portugal’s major Gothic buildings. Some date the start of its construction to 1189, the year of the first Christian conquest. Most historians place it in the 13th and 14th centuries instead. Go inside before heading up to the castle: the visit takes half an hour.

Known as Shilb, Silves was one of the important cities of western al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled Iberian Peninsula. The Museu Municipal de Arqueologia, which opened in 1990, tells the story of this period. It is built around a well dating from the Almohads, a Muslim dynasty from North Africa. You can view this well, 18 m deep and 4 m wide, through a glass floor. Stop here before visiting the castle: the objects on display help you imagine the Muslim city.

The Cruz de Portugal, a Gothic cross of white limestone about 3 m tall, stands on the outskirts of Silves, on the road to São Bartolomeu de Messines. One side depicts Christ on the cross; the other, a Pietà, with the Virgin holding her dead son. It is said to have been a gift from King Manuel I in 1499, but its origin remains uncertain. Allow ten minutes for a stop by car.

activities.text: Head to Faro Airport on the morning of your departure. Allow extra time to return the rental car.

practical_info.tip: Leave at least three hours before your flight to allow for a possible traffic jam on the A22.

seo.h1_title: Algarve in 7 Days: Ria Formosa, Benagil, Lagos, and Sagres
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7-day itinerary crosses the Algarve from east to west, with two bases, Tavira followed by Lagos, starting and ending in Faro. Take a boat to Culatra Island in the Ria Formosa lagoon, follow the Benagil cliffs along the Seven Hanging Valleys Trail, then continue to Ponta da Piedade and Cape St. Vincent. On the seventh day, head up into the Serra de Monchique, then stop at the red castle in Silves.
seo.seo_hook: Explore the Algarve in 7 days: boat trips to the Ria Formosa islands, Tavira, Benagil Cave, the cliffs of Lagos, and Cape St. Vincent.
featured_list: Faro: the Sé and its tower with about 68 steps overlooking the Ria Formosa
Olhão: red brick market halls and a boat trip to Culatra Island
Tavira: cemetery of 203 anchors at Praia do Barril
Benagil: cave with an opening in its ceiling, with no disembarking allowed since 2024
Lagos: Ponta da Piedade rock formations and the museum of the 1444 slave market
Sagres: Cape St. Vincent, 75 m cliffs, and an 1846 lighthouse
Monchique and Silves: Fóia at 902 m and a red sandstone castle

places_taglines.PT::faro: Fortified old town, cathedral, and chapel lined with 1,245 skulls.
places_taglines.PT::olhao: Fishing port with flat roofs, gateway to the islands.
places_taglines.PT::tavira: Town with 37 churches, a seven-arch bridge, and a beach with anchors.
places_taglines.PT::benagil: Fishing village at the foot of the cave with an opening in its ceiling.
places_taglines.PT::lagos: Port of the Age of Discovery, ramparts, and Ponta da Piedade rock formations.
places_taglines.PT::sagres: Henry the Navigator’s fortress, near Cape St. Vincent, Europe’s southwestern tip.
places_taglines.PT::monchique: Mountain town below Fóia, the highest point in the Algarve.
places_taglines.PT::silves: Former Muslim town dominated by a red sandstone castle.

highlights: Ria Formosa: 60 km of protected coastline, five sand islands, and two peninsulas
Algar de Benagil: sea cave with a collapsed ceiling, accessible by boat or guided kayak tour since 2024
Seven Hanging Valleys Trail: 5.7 km cliffside trail between Marinha and Vale Centeanes
Cape St. Vincent: southwestern tip of mainland Europe, with 75 m cliffs

itineraries.title: Óbidos, Nazaré, Alcobaça, Batalha, and Tomar in 6 Days
itineraries.subtitle: Travel from Óbidos to Tomar in 6 days via Peniche, Nazaré, the monasteries of Alcobaça and Batalha, and then Fátima.
itineraries.notes: Several museums close on Mondays (Óbidos, Peniche, the Aljubarrota center, and the Tomar synagogue): starting on a Tuesday avoids these closures. Boats to the Berlengas generally run from April to October, depending on the operator and sea conditions, and Nazaré’s giant waves form mainly from October to March.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May, June, or September: on the coast, average highs range from about 22 to 26 °C (based on climate normals for Alcobaça). In July and August, inland areas get hotter, with an average high of about 31 °C in Santarém, south of Tomar. From October to January, expect rainfall exceeding 100 mm per month, but this is also the season for Nazaré’s giant waves.

activities.text: You’ll start your drive in Lisbon, where you’ll pick up your rental car downtown or at the airport. The airport is about 7 km northeast of the historic center. From the capital, the A8 highway heads north and reaches Óbidos in just over an hour. Leave early to arrive in Óbidos before the tour buses bringing day-trippers from Lisbon.

practical_info.tip: Ideally, start on a Tuesday: several museums along the route close on Mondays (Óbidos, Peniche, the Aljubarrota center, and the Tomar synagogue).

visits.text: Blue-and-white tiles frame the small balcony of the Porta da Vila, the main entrance through Óbidos’s defensive walls. These Baroque-style azulejos (painted earthenware tiles) surround an oratory (a small prayer niche) dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade, the town’s patron saint. This is a double gateway: you pass through two successive openings before entering the town. Go before 10 AM to photograph it without the crowds.

The best view of Óbidos is from the wall walk along the Muralhas de Óbidos, the walkway atop the defensive walls that encircle the entire town. You can walk for more than a kilometer above the rooftops and narrow streets. Looking outward, you’ll see the 16th-century aqueduct, built at the request of Queen Catherine of Austria. The castle, now a place to stay, is reserved for its guests. Take care: the walkway has no guardrails, so hold children by the hand and come down before dark.

In 1441, King Afonso V married his cousin Isabel in the Igreja de Santa Maria in Óbidos. The bride and groom were 9 and 10 years old. This church, the town’s main church, has walls covered in 17th-century azulejos. It also houses paintings by the Baroque painter Josefa de Óbidos and her father, Baltazar Gomes Figueira. Afterward, look at the embroidery sold in town: since the 1950s, it has reproduced the motifs on these tiles.

The Museu Municipal de Óbidos, on Rua Direita, tells the story of the town’s artistic and religious history. Opened in 1970, it mainly displays paintings from the 16th and 17th centuries. The highlights are works by Josefa de Óbidos (1630–1684), who adopted the town’s name as her name as a painter. The museum is open from 9:30 AM to 1 PM and from 2 PM to 5:30 PM, and is closed on Mondays.

A church filled with books: Livraria de Santiago occupies a former 12th-century church inside Óbidos’s defensive walls. This choice is no coincidence. Since 2015, Óbidos has been part of UNESCO’s Cities of Literature network, and the town has more than ten bookstores. Step inside to browse the shelves, even if you don’t buy anything: admission is free.

You’ll head outside the defensive walls to the Santuário do Senhor Jesus da Pedra, a Baroque church with a hexagonal, or six-sided, floor plan. Construction, overseen by Captain Rodrigo Franco, began in 1740 and was completed around 1747. The towers never received the pinnacles (small stone points) planned for their tops, giving the building its unfinished appearance. Inside, a stone cross carved with the crucified Christ gave the sanctuary its name. Allow for a short detour by car from the Porta da Vila.

activities.text: If you try just one specialty in Óbidos, choose ginjinha served in a small chocolate cup. Ginjinha is a liqueur made by steeping sour cherries in brandy. Once you’ve finished the drink, you eat the cup. The counters along Rua Direita serve it plain, in chocolate, or “com ginja,” meaning with a cherry at the bottom.

practical_info.tip: This is strong liquor: limit yourself to one glass if you’ll be driving again.

activities.text: The Lagoa de Óbidos, northwest of town, forms the largest lagoon system on the Portuguese coast. A lagoon is a shallow body of water separated from the ocean by a sandbar: here, the average depth is no more than 2 m. Migratory birds stop mainly in the Barrosa arm to the east, and flamingos visit in winter. A trail, the Ecovia da Lagoa, follows its shores. Come late in the day with binoculars.

practical_info.tip: Boat trips depart near Covão dos Musaranhos; paddleboarding is available to the south, near Praia do Bom Sucesso.

visits.text: From 1934 to 1974, the Fortaleza de Peniche served as a political prison under the Estado Novo, Portugal’s dictatorship. Nearly 2,700 political prisoners were held here. On January 3, 1960, Communist leader Álvaro Cunhal and nine fellow prisoners escaped by climbing down the walls on a rope made from sheets. Opened in the fortress in 2024, the Museu Nacional Resistência e Liberdade lets visitors explore the cells and visiting room. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 AM to 6 PM; admission is €10.

You’ll end the day at Cabo Carvoeiro, the western tip of the Peniche peninsula, facing the Berlengas islands. A 25 m lighthouse guides ships from this headland, known for its shipwrecks. Right beside it stands the Nau dos Corvos, an isolated rock whose name means “the carrack of the crows” (a carrack was a large sailing ship used in earlier centuries). Come at sunset, but stay well back from the cliff edges.

activities.text: The trip’s most beautiful excursion starts at the port of Peniche: the crossing to Berlenga Grande, the main island in the Berlengas archipelago, about 15 kilometers offshore. The boat takes 40 to 45 minutes. On the island, a staircase leads to the Forte de São João Baptista, a 17th-century fort connected to the island by a bridge. The archipelago has been a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 2011, a designation that protects its natural environment: stay on marked trails. The island is limited to 550 visitors at any one time; this is not a quota for the entire day. Book early.

practical_info.tip: Boats run from early May to late September (in 2027, from May 8 to September 30 with Viamar), allowing about 5 hours on the island. Before boarding, register on the ICNF’s BerlengasPass platform and pay the €3 fee per person. Bring water, food, cash, and motion sickness medication if you’re prone to seasickness.

map_keywords: Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo Nazaré

visits.text: Locals in Nazaré tell how, in 1182, the knight Dom Fuas Roupinho was hunting a deer in the fog when his horse stopped short at the edge of the cliff. He credited the Virgin Mary with saving him and had the small Ermida da Memória, the “Chapel of Remembrance,” built on the spot. Its interior is covered with 17th- and 18th-century azulejos. Right beside it, the Miradouro do Suberco viewpoint overlooks the entire beach. Head up early to enjoy the view before the tour groups arrive.

The Santuário de Nossa Senhora da Nazaré overlooks the large square in Sítio. King Fernando I had a large church built here in 1377. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, it was transformed into a Baroque building, with interior walls covered in azulejos. It houses the statue of the Virgin Mary associated with the legend of Dom Fuas, the knight saved at the edge of the cliff. In the square, women vendors sometimes wear the traditional outfit with layered petticoats, known as the “seven skirts.” Cover your shoulders to enter: this is a pilgrimage site.

If you visit between October and March, watch the swell from the Forte de São Miguel Arcanjo, above Praia do Norte. This is where Nazaré’s giant waves form. Offshore, an underwater canyon about 230 km long plunges to a depth of 5,000 m. It begins 1 km from shore and channels the swell toward this beach. In 2020, Germany’s Sebastian Steudtner surfed a 26.2 m wave here, about the height of an eight-story building. In rough seas, stay on high ground: visitors have drowned on the beach.

The smell of salt and fish signals your arrival at the Museu do Peixe Seco, on the waterfront promenade. This living, open-air museum showcases a Nazaré tradition: drying fish in the sun. Horse mackerel (fish related to mackerel), sardines, small sharks, and octopuses are gutted, washed, and salted. They then dry for two to three days on wooden racks called estendais. Stop by in the morning to see the whole process, and buy a bag from the women vendors for a taste.

activities.text: The Ascensor da Nazaré, which takes you to Sítio, the old neighborhood perched on the cliff, has been closed for maintenance since November 9, 2026. The closure is expected to last about a month; the operator will announce the reopening date. This funicular, in service since 1889, travels 318 m on a 42% grade, rising 42 m for every 100 m horizontally. During the closure, you can walk up and back down along the Ladeira do Sítio, the old path between the beach and Sítio. The advertised one-way funicular fare is €2.50 in 2026.

practical_info.tip: The funicular sometimes closes for maintenance, as it did in fall 2025; when it does, you can walk up along the Ladeira do Sítio.

activities.text: Praia da Nazaré retains a slightly retro charm that makes it endearing. On the sand, rows of small canvas tents called barraquinhas face one another instead of the sea, encouraging conversations between neighbors. Outside the cultural center, old fishing boats are displayed outdoors, free to view. One was used for xávega, a fishing method in which teams of men and women hauled a net in from the beach.

practical_info.tip: The Blue Flag, a certification of water and beach quality, flies here from June 20 to September 15.

activities.text: Next, head to Pederneira, Nazaré’s third neighborhood, a former village built on a hill. From the Miradouro da Pederneira viewpoint, the view takes in the beach, Sítio on its cliff, and the lighthouse fort in the distance. This is the reverse of the view from Sítio, seen from the other side of the bay. Save this viewpoint for the end of the day, after the beach.

practical_info.tip: The viewpoint is outdoors, and no ticket is required.

activities.text: The Mercado Municipal de Nazaré reopened in April 2026 after renovations. This is where you’ll find the freshest fish in town, alongside fruit and vegetable stalls. Look for the day’s catch so you’ll know what to order later at a restaurant. Go in the morning, when the stalls are best stocked.

practical_info.tip: Combine the market with the Museu do Peixe Seco, close to the waterfront.

visits.text: At the heart of the Mosteiro de Alcobaça are two tombs in the transept, the part of the church that crosses the nave. They hold King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, his companion, who was murdered in 1355 on the orders of Pedro’s father. After becoming king, Pedro had her remains moved here. The two tombs face each other so that at the end of time, when the dead rise according to Christian belief, each will see the other first. On Pedro’s tomb, look for the inscription “Até ao fim do mundo,” meaning until the end of the world.

A channel diverted from the Alcoa River still runs through the kitchen of the Mosteiro de Alcobaça. The monks drew water and washed fish here without going outside. Above it, the enormous chimney rests on eight iron columns. The monastery, Portugal’s first Gothic building, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989. Its Claustro do Silêncio, commissioned by King Dinis in the late 13th century, was where the monks walked without speaking. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes, including the dormitory and the Hall of Kings.

activities.text: Finish your visit to Alcobaça with a sweet treat on the monastery square. Convent sweets, made with egg yolks and sugar, originated in convent kitchens. Try a cornucópia, a crisp pastry horn filled with egg custard, or trouxas de ovos, rolls of egg threads in syrup. Every November, the town hosts an international exhibition of convent sweets and liqueurs.

practical_info.tip: The monastery is open from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. from April through September and from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from October through March, with last admission 30 minutes before closing. The ticket price rose to €15 in 2025.

map_keywords: Centro de Interpretação da Batalha de Aljubarrota

visits.text: The Mosteiro da Batalha began with a vow: King João I had it built to thank the Virgin Mary for his victory over the Castilians at Aljubarrota in 1385. Construction lasted from 1386 to 1517. The Capela do Fundador is Portugal’s first royal pantheon, meaning its first burial chapel for kings. João I and the English queen Philippa of Lancaster rest beneath its star vault. One of their sons, Henry the Navigator, rests along the south wall. The monastery opens at 9 a.m. year-round.

Between 1448 and 1477, the Claustro Real at the Mosteiro da Batalha took on its Gothic form. Later, architect Mateus Fernandes added delicate stone screens between the arches in the Manueline style, Portugal’s decorative style of the early 16th century. Their motifs alternate between the cross of the Order of Christ and the armillary sphere, an astronomical instrument made of interlocking rings. Walk slowly around the cloister to spot these two motifs.

Two motionless sentries stand guard in the Sala do Capítulo, the chapter house of the Mosteiro da Batalha. They watch over the tomb of two unknown soldiers killed during World War I. Look up: the star vault spans about 19 m without a central pillar. It held only on the third attempt, and architect Huguet is said to have spent a night beneath it to prove its strength. Remain silent near the honor guard.

The most surprising part of the Mosteiro da Batalha was never completed: the Capelas Imperfeitas, the “Unfinished Chapels.” King Duarte began them around 1434 as a pantheon for his family, with seven burial chapels. The central vault was never built, leaving the space open to the sky. The tomb of Duarte and Queen Leonor was installed here in the 1940s. The entrance is outside the church; bring an umbrella if it rains.

activities.text: Between Alcobaça and Batalha, stop at the Centro de Interpretação da Batalha de Aljubarrota, on the São Jorge plateau. This is where the army of João I and Nuno Álvares Pereira defeated the Castilian army on August 14, 1385. A multimedia show lasting about 30 minutes tells the story of the battle. Near the neighboring chapel, a mass grave yielded nearly 2,900 bones damaged by arrows and crossbow bolts, which are short projectiles. The center is open from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. and is closed on Mondays.

practical_info.tip: Adult admission is about €7. Allow up to 2 hours 30 minutes to see everything, including the battlefield. Following Storm Kristin in January 2026, access to some areas of the monastery may remain limited; ask at reception.

visits.text: A cool temperature of around 17 °C welcomes you inside the Grutas de Mira de Aire, in summer and winter alike. Four local residents descended into the caves in 1947 in search of water. The caves opened to the public in 1974. The network extends for more than 11 km, but the tour covers about 600 m. You descend 683 steps to around 110 m underground, passing through chambers lit by colored lights. An elevator then takes you back to the surface. Tours start at 9:30 a.m., every day except December 25.

map_keywords: Monumento Natural das Pegadas de Dinossáurios da Serra de Aire

visits.text: Around 175 million years ago, sauropods walked across a mudflat here, an expanse of mud along the water’s edge. These long-necked herbivorous dinosaurs left around twenty trackways at the Monumento Natural das Pegadas de Dinossáurios da Serra de Aire, in the Parque Natural das Serras de Aire e Candeeiros. The two longest measure 147 m and 142 m. The round footprints were discovered in 1994 in a former quarry. The site is about ten kilometers from Fátima.

activities.text: You will then follow the roughly 1.8 km loop around the Pegadas de Dinossáurios quarry, with panels explaining the history of the Earth along the way. Before you head down, a 17-minute film places the tracks in the context of their time. The site’s garden brings together “living fossils,” ancient plants such as ferns, cycads (which look like small palm trees), and ginkgo, all of which already existed in the age of dinosaurs. Bring walking shoes.

practical_info.tip: Admission is €3 for adults and €2 for ages 6 to 12 and over 65. Hours differ between weekdays and weekends: check them before visiting.

visits.text: The Capelinha das Aparições, a small chapel at the heart of the Santuário de Fátima, marks the spot where three shepherd children said they saw the Virgin Mary in 1917. These apparitions took place from May 13 to October 13 of that year. Local residents began building the chapel in 1919. On the esplanade, some pilgrims move on their knees along a long strip of marble to fulfill a vow. On May 13 and October 13, crowds approach a million people: choose another date to move around freely.

The crackling of hundreds of candles accompanies your walk toward the Basílica de Nossa Senhora do Rosário, the white church with a colonnade on the esplanade. Its cornerstone was laid in 1928, and it was consecrated in 1953. It houses the tombs of the three children: Francisco and Jacinta Marto, who died of the flu in 1919 and 1920, and their cousin Lúcia, who died in 2005. Near the chapel, worshippers throw their candles into a large fire; expect to pay €0.50 to €2.70 per candle.

More surprising than beautiful at first glance, the Basílica da Santíssima Trindade is an immense modern circular hall on the other side of the esplanade. Dedicated on October 12, 2007, it measures about 125 m in diameter and 18 m in height. Each of its twelve bronze doors, around 9 m tall, bears a phrase from the Bible. Behind the altar stands a 3 m statue of the Virgin Mary in white Carrara marble. Visit outside service times to appreciate the scale of the space.

You will then walk to Aljustrel, the hamlet where the three children were born, just over 2 km from the sanctuary. Allow about 30 minutes on foot. The homes of Lúcia and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta have been preserved and are free to visit. They open daily from 9 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 5:45 p.m. Nearby, a monument at the Poço do Arneiro, an old well, marks the spot where, according to the children’s account, an angel appeared to them in 1916.

Angels, saints, and prophets carved in wood fill the Charola, the round church of the Convento de Cristo in Tomar. The Knights Templar, an order of warrior monks, built it in the 12th century, modeling it on the sanctuaries of Jerusalem. It has sixteen sides on the outside, with a drum, an eight-sided interior tower, rising at its center. In the 16th century, the vault and walls were covered with paintings, including depictions of the instruments of Christ’s Passion. Arrive when it opens at 9 a.m. to see it before the tour groups.

The Janela do Capítulo is the most symbolic of the five Manueline windows in the church of the Convento de Cristo. Manueline is a Portuguese decorative style from the early 16th century, rich in symbols associated with the Age of Discovery, the maritime voyages of the time. Diogo de Arruda designed its decoration. For the best view, look for the small cell facing it in the large dormitory. The convent has several cloisters, some of which reopened in 2026 after restoration: ask at reception which are open. Admission has been €15 since 2025.

If you have a car, drive five minutes from the convent to see the Aqueduto dos Pegões, the aqueduct that supplied it with water. It stretches for about 6 km and has 180 arches. In the Pegões valley, two tiers of arches rise to a height of 30 m. Designed by the Italian Filippo Terzi, it was completed in 1614, and water reached the main cloister in 1619. Admire it from the base of the arches: there are no guardrails at the top, and the structure sustained damage in the January 2026 storm.

You will then cross town to the Praça da República, Tomar’s main square, where a statue of Gualdim Pais stands prominently. This leader of the Knights Templar in Portugal laid the castle’s cornerstone in 1160, and the town celebrates him as its founder. Facing city hall, the Igreja de São João Baptista has an octagonal Manueline bell tower. Inside, look for the panels painted in the 1530s by Gregório Lopes. Look at the square’s paving, too: its patterns pay tribute to the Knights Templar.

In 1496, the expulsion of Jews from Portugal brought services at the Sinagoga de Tomar, built in the 15th century, to an end. Tomar’s tourist office describes it as the oldest synagogue in the country. Four columns support the vault, representing the four biblical matriarchs: Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, and Rachel. The twelve corbels on the walls, small stone supports, evoke the twelve tribes. Clay jars embedded in the walls improved the acoustics. It houses the Abraão Zacuto Museum, open Tuesday through Sunday.

Tomar’s most moving church is also its most unassuming: the Igreja de Santa Maria do Olival. This 13th-century Gothic church served as the pantheon of the Templar masters, meaning their burial place. The tombstone of Gualdim Pais, the town’s founder, is still there. The building stands on the site of a former Benedictine monastery. Opening hours vary: check with the tourist office before visiting.

activities.text: Finally, you will walk along the Nabão, the river that flows through Tomar. The Levada is a canal fed by the river. Along its banks, former grain mills and olive presses now form a cultural complex. A charter issued by Gualdim Pais in 1162 already mentions mills here. In Mouchão Park, on a small island, a wooden waterwheel dating from 1906 still lifts water in clay buckets. From the park, the view takes in the Ponte Velha and the Templar castle.

practical_info.tip: Every four years in July, the Festa dos Tabuleiros fills these streets with women carrying tall trays of bread and flowers on their heads. The most recent festival took place in 2023.

visits.text: The Castelo de Almourol occupies a rocky islet in the middle of the Tagus. It can only be reached by boat, as there is no bridge or walking route. According to the inscription above the gate, the Knights Templar rebuilt it starting in 1171 under the direction of Gualdim Pais, the founder of Tomar. The castle guarded the river during the Reconquista, the recapture of lands from Muslim rule. The boat leaves from the Cais de Almourol, facing the castle, with no reservation required; tickets cost €4.

activities.text: To learn about the castle’s history before or after the crossing, stop by the Centro de Interpretação Templário de Almourol (CITA). It is located in the cultural center in Vila Nova da Barquinha, about 4 km away. This center is devoted to the Knights Templar and their defensive line along the Tagus. Admission is included in the castle ticket. Hours vary by season and day: confirm them in advance.

practical_info.tip: The castle is open from 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. from March through September, and from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2:30 p.m. to 5 p.m. from October through February. The last crossing is 40 minutes before closing; visits are suspended when river conditions are unsafe.

activities.text: You’ll drive from Almourol to Lisbon on the highway in about 1 hour 20 minutes to return the car at the airport or downtown. The airport is about 7 km northeast of the historic center, so you can avoid driving across the entire city. Allow extra time to fill up the tank and return the car before your flight.

practical_info.tip: Driving time is already included in the transfer from Almourol.

seo.h1_title: Óbidos, Nazaré, Alcobaça, Batalha, and Tomar in 6 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: This 6-day itinerary from Lisbon connects Óbidos, Peniche, and Nazaré on the coast, then the monasteries of Alcobaça and Batalha. It continues through the Mira de Aire caves, the dinosaur footprints of Serra de Aire, and Fátima before reaching Tomar and Almourol Castle. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie along the route.
seo.seo_hook: Óbidos’s defensive walls, Nazaré’s waves, the monasteries of Alcobaça and Batalha, and Tomar’s Knights Templar: 6 days in central Portugal.
featured_list: Óbidos: over a kilometer of defensive walls and a church converted into a bookstore
Peniche: boat crossing to the Berlengas, a UNESCO biosphere reserve
Nazaré: giant waves from October through March below the lighthouse fort
Alcobaça: the facing tombs of Pedro and Inês
Batalha: a 19 m vault without a central pillar
Tomar: the Knights Templar’s 12th-century Charola

places_taglines.PT::lisboa: Starting and ending point, with the airport 7 km from the center.
places_taglines.PT::obidos: Fortified town with accessible defensive walls, a UNESCO City of Literature.
places_taglines.PT::peniche: Fishing port, former political prison, and departure point for the Berlengas.
places_taglines.PT::nazare: Fishing town where the giant waves of Praia do Norte form.

itineraries.title: Douro in 5 Days: Quintas, Pinhão, and the Côa Rock Engravings
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, follow the Douro from Amarante to Pinhão by boat and train, then head to the Côa rock engravings.
itineraries.notes: The Côa rock engravings can only be visited with a guide, by 4x4, and with advance reservations: book Penascosa (in the afternoon) and Canada do Inferno (in the morning) as soon as your dates are set. The grape harvest runs from September to mid-October: the quintas are especially lively then, so book the cruise and wine tasting ahead as well.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May, June, September, and October, with afternoon temperatures of 23 to 29 °C in Régua (1981–2010 averages). Avoid July and August, when temperatures average around 32 °C and sometimes climb much higher: Pinhão recorded 47 °C on July 14, 2022, Portugal’s record for the month of July. From November through January, rainfall exceeds 100 mm per month, and the Régua–Pinhão cruise season generally runs from April through October, depending on the operator.

activities.text: Leave Porto on the A4 highway toward Amarante, 63 km away. Before setting off, step into the main hall of São Bento station. Its roughly 20,000 azulejos, painted ceramic tiles installed between 1905 and 1916, offer a first glimpse of the grape harvest and wine transport on the Douro. The Douro train departs from here, but in 2026 buses replace it along part of the route, so driving remains the simpler option.

practical_info.tip: The main hall of São Bento station is free to enter: ten minutes is enough to see all the tile panels.

visits.text: In 1809, soldiers and residents of Amarante defended the Ponte de São Gonçalo against Napoleon’s troops for fourteen days. The current bridge dates to 1790: it replaced an older bridge swept away by a flood of the Tâmega in 1763. Traces of the fighting are still visible on the stone. Walk across, then sit on a bench in one of its four small semicircular overlooks, facing the river and São Gonçalo Church.

The facade of the Igreja de São Gonçalo is worth looking up at. The Varanda dos Reis, the “balcony of kings,” displays statues of four 16th-century monarchs, including Philip I, king of Spain, who also became king of Portugal in 1581. Inside, a statue of the saint, who died in 1262, stands on his tomb. São Gonçalo is believed to help single women find a husband: many still come to pray or leave flowers. Allow time for the neighboring cloister, which houses the municipal museum.

Amarante is a small town, but its museum tells the story of a modern painter with ties to the Cubists whose recognition reached as far as New York. The Museu Municipal Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso, housed in the cloister of the former convent, honors this painter, born in Amarante in 1887 and a friend of Modigliani in Paris. In 1913, he sold seven of the eight paintings he exhibited at the Armory Show, a modern art exhibition in New York. He died of the Spanish flu in 1918, at age 30. The museum is closed on Mondays and between 12:30 p.m. and 2 p.m.

activities.text: Egg yolks, sugar, and almonds: this trio gives the cakes at Confeitaria da Ponte their sweetness. Opened in 1930, it is Amarante’s oldest pastry shop. Its recipes come from the town’s former convents. Try the lérias (egg yolks and almonds), foguetes (egg-filled puff pastries), and brisas do Tâmega (small boat-shaped pastries filled with egg cream). Expect to pay one to two euros apiece, to take out or enjoy on the terrace.

practical_info.tip: It is at 186 Rua 31 de Janeiro, overlooking the Tâmega.

to_next_leg.road_type: A4 through the Marão tunnel, then N313

visits.text: “A boat with its keel in the air”: Portuguese writer Miguel Torga saw this hill as an overturned boat hull in the middle of the valley. At the Miradouro de São Leonardo de Galafura, at an elevation of 640 m, an azulejo panel reproduces his text near the chapel. Below, terraced vineyards descend to the Douro. For a picnic, stone tables await in the shade a little farther down.

map_keywords: Museu do Douro Peso da Régua

visits.text: The Museu do Douro occupies the Casa da Companhia, an 18th-century building restored and turned into a museum in 2008. It belonged to the company established in 1756 to regulate Douro wine production. This company marked the boundaries of the wine-growing area with granite boundary stones to better control production. The permanent exhibition tells the story of this landscape through tools, bottle labels, and works of art. Finish on the garden terrace above the river. The museum is open daily, with admission costing €7.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip, choose the cruise from Régua to Pinhão, which heads up the Douro in a little over two hours. The highlight is the lock at Bagaúste Dam. The boat enters a large chamber enclosed by gates, which is then filled with water: the boat rises about 27 m to the level of the river upstream of the dam. This passage takes half an hour. Departures are in the afternoon, at around €30 per adult.

practical_info.tip: The cruise departs from the Régua dock and operates mainly from May through October. Book online in advance.

activities.text: Return from Pinhão to Régua on the Douro railway line, following the water for about 25 minutes. The first train arrived in Régua in 1879. The Portuguese rail company describes this line as the only one in the world linking three UNESCO sites: Porto’s city center, the Douro wine-growing region, and the Côa rock engravings. Buy your ticket at Pinhão station or on board.

practical_info.tip: Trains are infrequent: check cp.pt to make sure the last train to Régua leaves after the boat arrives.

to_next_leg.road_type: N222 along the Douro, 93 curves in 27 km

visits.text: Few train stations are worth a stop in their own right, but Pinhão’s is. Its walls feature 24 blue-and-white azulejo panels, made up of more than 3,000 ceramic tiles manufactured in Aveiro and installed in 1937. They depict vineyard work, grape treading, and rabelos, the wooden boats that carried wine downriver to the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from Porto. Come early in the morning to see them without the crowds, then stop by the station’s wine shop.

If you visit just one viewpoint around Pinhão, choose the Miradouro de Casal de Loivos. From this village perched at around 490 m, you can see the Douro sweeping through a broad bend between the terraces, with Pinhão far below. It is just a ten-minute drive, but the streets are narrow and parking is very difficult. Walkers can hike up from the station: the loop is 6 km, with 340 m of elevation gain, and takes a little over 2 hours. Come early in the morning or at sunset.

activities.text: Cross Pinhão’s bridge to reach Quinta das Carvalhas on the other bank of the Douro. Its vineyards climb from 80 m at the water’s edge to an elevation of 400 m. The estate was already mentioned in written records in 1759. With a map in hand, follow a marked trail uphill through vineyards, terraces, and olive groves. The experience ends with a port tasting and costs €10 per adult. Book a time slot on the quinta’s website: in summer, choose 10 a.m., before the heat sets in.

practical_info.tip: Time slots at 10 a.m., 2 p.m., and 4 p.m. (the last is available only from March through October). Closed December 24–26 and January 1–2.

activities.text: Since 1896, Quinta do Bomfim, beside the village on the banks of the Douro, has produced Dow’s ports. The tour takes you through the old wine cellar, then past modern lagares: these vats were designed to imitate traditional grape treading by foot. It ends with a tasting overlooking the river. From September to early October, you can see the grape harvest, done by hand. Book ahead, especially during this period.

practical_info.tip: Open daily, 10 a.m.–7 p.m. from March through October and 9:30 a.m.–6:30 p.m. in winter. Closed December 25, January 1, and July 4.

map_keywords: Museu do Côa Vila Nova de Foz Côa
Parish Church of Vila Nova de Foz Côa

visits.text: From a distance, the Museu do Côa looks less like a museum than a large boulder emerging from the hillside. Its architects, Camilo Rebelo and Tiago Pimentel, tinted the concrete with mineral pigments to imitate the region’s rocks. Opened in 2010, it overlooks the point where the Côa flows into the Douro. Its seven galleries explain the valley’s rock art: images engraved on rocks in the open air. From November through March, it is closed on Mondays.

The first thing you notice about the Igreja Matriz de Vila Nova de Foz Côa is its portal: five carved arches nested inside one another. This is the Manueline style, the Portuguese decorative style of the early 16th century named after King Manuel I. In the chancel, the ceiling is divided into 27 coffers, square compartments painted with scenes from the lives of Christ and the Virgin Mary. Right beside the church stands the pillory, a stone column that symbolized municipal authority. Stop by toward the end of the day, on your way back from Penascosa.

activities.text: The 4x4 bumps along 6 km of dirt track between almond and olive trees, then stops beside the Côa at the Penascosa site. Between 22,000 and 10,000 BCE, the valley’s engravers mainly depicted horses, aurochs (now-extinct wild cattle), and wild goats. Here, one horse has three overlapping heads: as the light shifts across the rock, it seems to turn its head. The guided tour leaves Castelo Melhor, 15 km from Foz Côa, in the afternoon and costs €18.

practical_info.tip: Book through the park (visitas@arte-coa.pt): visitor numbers are limited each day. A nighttime tour by flashlight is also available for €22.

visits.text: In 1640, the residents of Castelo Rodrigo set fire to their own lord’s palace. Cristóvão de Moura had it built in 1590 at the top of the village. This diplomat had helped the king of Spain take the Portuguese throne in 1580. When Portugal regained its own king in 1640, the palace became a symbol of sixty years of Spanish rule. Only ruins remain, at the end of the narrow streets. Enter the walled enclosure through the Porta do Sol, the main gate, which faces east.

In Castelo Rodrigo, you will pass the medieval cistern, a water reservoir dug 13 m deep. One of its two doorways, with a horseshoe arch, is thought to date from the late 10th century. Farther on, the Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Rocamador, mentioned in records as early as 1209, welcomed pilgrims on their way to Santiago de Compostela. Also look for a Hebrew inscription dated 1508 on a doorframe: it recalls the village’s Jewish community.

For a sweeping view of the entire Côa region, nothing beats the Serra da Marofa, the mountain overlooking Castelo Rodrigo. At an elevation of 977 m, a statue of Christ the King about 6 m tall spreads its arms above the fields, forests, and villages. A 7 km road climbs here from Figueira de Castelo Rodrigo, the neighboring town. Choose a clear day, then head back down toward Foz Côa.

map_keywords: Canada do Inferno Vila Nova de Foz Côa

activities.text: “As gravuras não sabem nadar”—“the engravings can’t swim”: this slogan saved Canada do Inferno. This is where the first Côa rock engravings were spotted in late 1991. A dam was being built at the time, and its reservoir would have submerged them. In November 1995, the government abandoned the project. UNESCO added the valley to its World Heritage List in 1998. On rock No. 1, a horse has two heads. The goat on rock No. 14 serves as the park’s logo.

practical_info.tip: Departures from the Museu do Côa, mornings only, by 4x4 (€18). Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours, with about 800 m of walking, including steps. Book ahead.

map_keywords: Wine Cellars Vila Nova de Gaia

activities.text: You return to Porto after a drive of about 2 hours 30 minutes from Vila Nova de Foz Côa. For many years, the ports you tasted in Pinhão ended their journey just across the Douro, in the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia. This is where the rabelos delivered the barrels brought down from the valley. If you have the afternoon free, cross the river to visit one of these cellars and complete the wine’s journey.

practical_info.tip: Gaia’s wine cellars offer tours with tastings: book ahead in peak season.

seo.h1_title: Douro in 5 Days: Quintas, Pinhão, and the Côa Rock Engravings
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day road trip starts in Porto and follows the Douro through its wine-growing region, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. After Amarante and the São Leonardo de Galafura viewpoint, you travel upriver from Régua to Pinhão by boat, return downriver by train, and visit two quintas, or wine estates. The final days take you to Vila Nova de Foz Côa, where you can visit rock engravings more than 12,000 years old on a guided 4x4 tour.
seo.seo_hook: Amarante, the Douro Museum, a cruise and train ride to Pinhão, a tasting at a quinta, and the Côa rock engravings: the Douro Valley in 5 days from Porto.
featured_list: Amarante: São Gonçalo Bridge, defended for fourteen days against Napoleon in 1809
Peso da Régua: the Douro Museum and a cruise to Pinhão through the Bagaúste lock
Pinhão: 24 azulejo panels installed in the train station in 1937
Vale do Côa: rock engravings added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998
Castelo Rodrigo: Cristóvão de Moura’s palace, burned down in 1640

places_taglines.PT::sao-leonardo-de-galafura: A viewpoint at 640 m overlooking the Douro’s terraced vineyards.
places_taglines.PT::peso-da-regua: The Douro Museum and the departure point for the cruise to Pinhão.
places_taglines.PT::pinhao: A train station with azulejos from 1937, port wine quintas, and a viewpoint.
places_taglines.PT::vila-nova-de-foz-coa: The Côa Museum and rock engravings added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998.
places_taglines.PT::castelo-rodrigo: A fortified village, a palace burned down in 1640, and a medieval cistern.

Museu do Côa: opened in 2010 above the confluence of the Côa and Douro rivers
