itineraries.title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo
itineraries.subtitle: In 7 days, travel from Funchal to Pico Ruivo, the levadas of Rabaçal, and the lava pools of Porto Moniz.
itineraries.notes: Since January 1, 2026, every designated trail must be booked through the SIMplifica portal (€4.50 per trail for nonresidents over 12), and the regional forest service (IFCN) closes them all during weather alerts. Ideally, start on a Sunday: the market, the sacred art museum, and the carros de cesto do not operate on Sundays, and both MUDAS and Quinta das Cruzes are closed on Sundays and Mondays.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: April through June and September, with afternoon temperatures of 21 to 27 °C in Funchal and very little rain from May through September. From October through February, expect 65 to 95 mm of rain per month on the south coast, and more in the mountains, where the forest service closes the trails whenever a weather alert is issued. At Pico do Areeiro and Pico Ruivo, bring a warm jacket year-round: clouds are frequent, and snow is possible in winter above 1,200 m.

activities.text: You will land at Cristiano Ronaldo Madeira Airport, in the municipality of Santa Cruz, 13 km from Funchal. Its runway runs alongside the ocean: the extension, completed in 2000, rests on 180 columns around 70 m tall. Wind often disrupts air traffic here, so delays are possible. Pick up your rental car, then follow the expressway west: central Funchal is about 20 minutes away.

practical_info.tip: Create your account on the SIMplifica portal as soon as you arrive: since January 1, 2026, every designated trail (PR) must be booked for a 30-minute time slot.

visits.text: The finest feature of Sé do Funchal, the cathedral, is above your head. It is a cedarwood ceiling in the Mudéjar style, a decorative style that originated among Muslim artisans in Christian Spain. Construction began in 1486 using volcanic stone from Cabo Girão, a cliff you will see near the end of your trip. In the choir stalls, the wooden seats reserved for the clergy, look for bananas and wineskins carved among the prophets. Visit outside Mass times.

Doors turned into paintings line Rua de Santa Maria in the heart of Zona Velha, Funchal’s old town. Funchal’s first inhabitants settled in this neighborhood. The Arte Portas Abertas project (“open-door art”) had around 200 doors of abandoned houses and shops painted. Walk past Capela do Corpo Santo, a 15th-century chapel. A little farther on, Fortaleza de São Tiago, a fort begun in 1614, protected the city from privateers. In the evening, the street’s outdoor dining areas come alive.

activities.text: Deliberately heated, Madeira wine can keep for more than 200 years in the bottle. Heat and air, which damage other wines, make this wine very stable, even after the bottle is opened. At Blandy’s Wine Lodge, in cellars dating from the 17th and 18th centuries, you will learn how this method originated: in the past, wine crossed the tropics in ships’ holds and returned tasting better. Fine wines, meanwhile, age without heating in warm rooms, using the canteiro method. Taste a Sercial, the driest, followed by a Malvasia, the sweetest.

practical_info.tip: Open daily; closed from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m. on Sundays.

map_keywords: Museu de Arte Sacra do Funchal

visits.text: The Museu de Arte Sacra do Funchal occupies the former bishop’s palace, founded in 1594. Its surprise is a collection of large-scale Flemish paintings, uncommon in European museums. From the 15th century onward, Madeira’s sugar was sold in Bruges and Antwerp. Enriched by this trade, the island’s plantation owners and merchants commissioned expensive works in Flanders. Allow 1 hour; the museum is closed on Sundays and closes at 1:30 p.m. on Saturdays.

activities.text: If you visit just one market in Madeira, choose Mercado dos Lavradores, Funchal’s farmers’ market. The building, inaugurated in 1940 and designed by architect Edmundo Tavares, blends Art Deco and modernism. On the facade and in the fish hall, large panels of azulejos (painted ceramic tiles) by João Rodrigues depict scenes from the island. The fruit stalls are set up outdoors in the inner courtyard.

practical_info.tip: Come on a weekday morning: the market opens at 7 a.m., closes at 2 p.m. on Saturdays, and is closed on Sundays.

map_keywords: Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Monte

visits.text: Koi glide beneath pagodas and Buddha statues at Monte Palace Madeira, a 7-hectare tropical garden in the hills above Funchal. Along the paths is a collection of azulejos (painted ceramic tiles) dating from the 17th through the 20th centuries. Two permanent exhibitions round out the visit, one on Africa and the other on the treasures of nature. The Funchal cable car (Teleférico do Funchal) takes you up from Zona Velha in 15 minutes, climbing 560 m in elevation. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Austria’s last emperor rests in Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Monte, far from Vienna. Charles I died in exile in Funchal on April 1, 1922, at age 34. His body was placed in a chapel in this church, begun in 1741; his heart is kept in Switzerland. On August 15, the Feast of the Assumption, celebrated here since 1551, fills the square in front of the church. Visit the church just before the carros de cesto ride down from Monte.

Quieter than Monte Palace, Jardim Botânico da Madeira spreads across 8 hectares of terraces above Funchal. It opened in 1960 on the Reid family’s former estate, Quinta do Bom Sucesso. More than 2,000 exotic plants from every continent grow here. Viewpoints overlook the city. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; the garden closes at 5:30 p.m.

activities.text: You will reach the botanical garden from Monte on the Teleférico do Jardim Botânico in 9 minutes. Over a distance of 1,600 m, the cabin glides over the wooded Ribeira de João Gomes valley, between 10 and 100 m above the ground. Buy a round-trip ticket: the carros de cesto leave from Monte, so you will need to go back up there after visiting the garden.

practical_info.tip: Runs daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: In Madeira, they are called carros de cesto, or “basket cars.” These wicker sleds on wooden runners have been traveling down the road from Monte to Livramento since 1850: about 2 km in around 10 minutes. Two carreiros, drivers dressed in white and wearing straw boater hats, push the sled and then brake with their rubber soles. Despite having no engine, it reaches nearly 38 km/h on the slope.

practical_info.tip: Monday through Saturday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with no departures on Sundays or public holidays. In Livramento, plan to take a taxi to reach downtown.

activities.text: The PR8 Vereda da Ponta de São Lourenço trail starts at Baía d'Abra and follows the peninsula for 4 km to Casa do Sardinha. Look for the dark veins in the cliffs: lava that cooled in cracks in the rock. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes round-trip in full sun: bring water and a hat.

practical_info.tip: Book your time slot on the regional government’s SIMplifica portal: reservations for designated trails have been mandatory since January 1, 2026, and the access fee is €4.50 per person over age 12. The IFCN, the forest service, closes all trails during weather alerts: check their status on visitmadeira.com the day before. The headland has been a nature reserve since 1982: stay on the trail.

visits.text: In 1419, João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira landed on Machico beach before claiming Madeira for the Portuguese crown. In 1440, Machico became the archipelago’s first captaincy: a territory entrusted to Tristão Vaz and his descendants by Prince Henry the Navigator. On this volcanic island, the pale sand of Praia de Machico is a surprise: it was brought from Western Sahara. Go for a swim after hiking PR8; the beach is a 15-minute drive away.

map_keywords: Penha de Águia Porto da Cruz
Engenhos do Norte Porto da Cruz

visits.text: Penha de Águia, the “eagle’s rock,” is an escarpment rising to 580 m above sea level that towers over Porto da Cruz. The village grew with sugarcane, which the first settlers were already cultivating. For a photo, head down to the village waterfront.

activities.text: If you visit between March and May, you will see the machinery running at Engenhos do Norte in Porto da Cruz. Built in 1927 with 19th-century machinery, this mill still produces sugarcane spirit, Madeira rum, using the original methods. During the rest of the year, screens explain how the machinery works. Afterward, sample a few rums at Casa do Rum, right next door.

practical_info.tip: You can only see sugarcane being processed between March and May.

visits.text: Touristy but informative, the Casas Típicas de Santana show how farmers on the north coast once lived. Their thatched roofs, made from wheat and rye stalks, slope almost to the ground to shed rainwater; they are replaced every four to five years. Beneath the roof, the attic stored crops, while the ground floor housed a kitchen and a bedroom. The wooden facades are painted white, red, and blue. The entire municipality is designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

to_next_leg.justification: This is a substantial detour: from Santana, the road passes through Faial, Ribeiro Frio, and Poiso before climbing to Pico do Areeiro; 33 km in 50 minutes is realistic on these mountain roads.

visits.text: Park almost at the summit: a road leads up to Pico do Areeiro, Madeira’s third-highest peak (1,818 m). On clear days, the view extends across the ridges of the central massif, Ponta de São Lourenço, and the steep-sided Curral das Freiras valley; in exceptionally clear weather, you can see Porto Santo. Sunrise draws photographers here when the weather allows. Parking costs €4 per hour, and the road can be icy in winter.

activities.text: Walk the first section of PR1 Vereda do Areeiro to the Pedra Rija viewpoint (Miradouro da Pedra Rija), 1.2 km from the summit. The trail follows ridges of volcanic rock between steep slopes. Allow about 1 hour round-trip.

practical_info.tip: Book on SIMplifica: €4.50 as far as Pedra Rija, €10.50 for the full traverse. The full route (6.1 km, about 3 hours) passes through tunnels cut into tuff, a rock made of compacted volcanic ash, where shepherds and their flocks once sheltered. It ends at Pico Ruivo: arrange a taxi to get back to your car.

to_next_leg.justification: No road leads up to Pico Ruivo: the drive goes through Santana to the Achada do Teixeira parking lot, and the 2.8 km walk along the PR1.2 trail is already included in this stop’s itinerary.

visits.text: A sea of clouds can surround Pico Ruivo, Madeira’s highest point at 1,862 m. On clear days, the view extends as far as Porto Santo and the Desertas Islands. North of the summit, the mountain hut, renovated in 2019, offers water and meals to hikers. Bring a warm jacket for the climb, even in summer.

activities.text: The shortest route to Madeira’s highest point is also the easiest: the PR1.2 Vereda do Pico Ruivo starts at the Achada do Teixeira parking lot and reaches Pico Ruivo in 2.8 km. At the start, look for Homem em Pé, the “standing man,” a pillar of rock. Shelters along the trail offer protection from sudden weather changes, which are common at this altitude. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes round-trip, plus time at the summit.

practical_info.tip: Reserve a time slot on SIMplifica (€4.50). The trail is marked and equipped with guardrails. The IFCN closes trails during weather alerts: check their status on visitmadeira.com the day before.

to_next_leg.justification: This does involve a detour: descend from Achada do Teixeira toward Santana, then follow the north coast to São Vicente; 48 km in 70 minutes is consistent with the route planner’s estimate (45 km).

visits.text: A chapel inside a rock: in São Vicente, on the north coast, the Capela de São Vicente was built into a basalt boulder by the sea, near the river’s mouth. The rock protects it from the sea. Stop for 15 minutes to walk around it. The waves along this coast also attract surfers and bodyboarders.

Black sand, green cliffs, and Atlantic waves: Praia do Porto do Seixal formed naturally a few years ago beside the small harbor. This dark sand, made of volcanic rock, heats up quickly in the sun, so bring sandals. Showers, a bar, and kayak rentals are available on-site. Around the village, small vineyards cling to almost vertical terraces.

Miradouro do Véu da Noiva, the “bridal veil” viewpoint, overlooks the coast between São Vicente and Seixal. It faces a waterfall that plunges from the cliff above the old coastal road carved into the rock. Stay behind the barriers: water from the waterfall and falling rocks still land on this old road.

Save Aquário da Madeira, Porto Moniz’s aquarium, for a day with heavy swells. It occupies the Forte de São João Baptista, a fort built in 1730 to defend against pirate attacks and later restored by the municipality. Since 2005, its 12 tanks have showcased more than 90 species found around the archipelago; the largest holds 500,000 liters of seawater.

activities.text: Formed by lava that cooled at the ocean’s edge, the Piscinas Naturais do Porto Moniz are black rock pools with a constant flow of seawater. The water stays around 20 to 21 °C year-round. The developed complex, with pools about 2 m deep, offers changing rooms, a bar, and a children’s pool; admission costs €3. The pools beside the aquarium are free, but have no lifeguards.

practical_info.tip: In rough seas, the developed pools may close without notice: check the Porto Moniz municipal website before visiting.

to_next_leg.justification: The ER209 climbs in switchbacks from Porto Moniz to the Fanal plateau; 12 km in 25 minutes is realistic—the route planner’s speed of 18 km/h was too slow.

activities.text: Twisted trees with strange shapes stand apart from one another: in Fanal, many of the til trees (Ocotea foetens, a species of laurel) are more than a century old. This forest existed before the Portuguese arrived. It is part of the Laurissilva, Madeira’s UNESCO-protected laurel forest: a remnant of the forests that covered southern Europe 15 to 40 million years ago. In winter, a pond forms in an ancient crater. The site is designated an area for rest and silence: keep your voice down.

practical_info.tip: The PR13 Vereda do Fanal and PR14 Levada dos Cedros trails start here; reservations are required through SIMplifica. A picnic area with grills is available.

to_next_leg.justification: This does involve a detour: the route crosses the Paul da Serra plateau on the ER110 to the Rabaçal trailhead; 15 km in 20 minutes is realistic on this open plateau.

activities.text: The PR6 Levada das 25 Fontes follows a levada, an irrigation channel carved into the mountainside. Madeira has more than 2,170 km of levadas, and their maintenance paths now serve as hiking trails. The trail runs for 4.3 km through the laurel forest, with views of the Ribeira da Janela valley. At the end, water flowing down from the Paul da Serra plateau emerges from 25 springs around a pool. Allow about 3 hours round-trip, returning along the same trail.

practical_info.tip: Reserve your time slot through the regional government’s SIMplifica portal: reservations for designated trails have been mandatory since January 1, 2026, and the access fee is €4.50 per person over 12. The IFCN, the forest service, closes all trails during weather alerts: check their status on visitmadeira.com the day before. From the parking lot on the ER105, the narrow 2 km road down to the trailhead is closed to cars: walk or take the paid municipal shuttle.

activities.text: You’ll start from the same place for PR6.1 Levada do Risco, an easy 1.5 km trail that shares its opening stretch with PR6. At the end, Risco waterfall drops straight down, tracing a white line against the dark rock. On its own, the hike takes about 2 hours round-trip, but you can combine it with PR6 on the same day.

practical_info.tip: The ground gets muddy on rainy days: wear shoes with lugged soles.

to_next_leg.road_type: Descent from the plateau to the west coast

map_keywords: MUDAS Museu de Arte Contemporânea da Madeira

visits.text: The building alone makes MUDAS, Madeira’s contemporary art museum in Calheta, worth a visit. Designed by architect Paulo David, it sits on a hill above town. Its collection of about 400 works, dating from the 1960s to the present, was displayed at the Fortaleza de São Tiago in Funchal until 2015. Open Tuesday through Saturday, with a break from 1 p.m. to 2 p.m.; closed Sundays, Mondays, and public holidays.

activities.text: Madeira rum is also made in the west: Engenho da Calheta, one of the island’s oldest sugarcane mills, produces rum and mel de cana. This “cane honey” is a dark syrup made from sugarcane juice. Taste both on-site, in small quantities if you’re driving.

practical_info.tip: Allow 30 minutes for the tour and tasting.

activities.text: You’ll end the day at Praia de Areia da Calheta, a sandy beach near the marina and one of the busiest on the west coast. After the levadas of Rabaçal, this is the place for a swim before dinner.

practical_info.tip: Keep a swimsuit and towel in the car for this final stop of the day.

visits.text: Beneath the glass platform at Cabo Girão, a 580 m drop separates your feet from the ocean. Madeira’s tourism office describes it as Europe’s highest promontory. Below, Fajã do Rancho and Fajã do Cabo Girão, small patches of cultivated land at the foot of the cliff, look tiny. The volcanic stone used for Funchal Cathedral was quarried from this cliff. The viewpoint is open daily from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.; nonresidents over 12 pay an admission fee.

map_keywords: Miradouro do Espírito Santo Câmara de Lobos

visits.text: Here, the colorful fishing boats bobbing in the bay of Câmara de Lobos are called xavelhas. The town takes its name from the monk seals, known as lobos-marinhos (“sea wolves”), that Zarco found in this bay in 1419; only a small colony remains in the Desertas Islands. In January 1950, Winston Churchill set up his easel at Miradouro do Espírito Santo to paint facing the sea. Head up there to see the view from his vantage point.

activities.text: If you try just one local drink, choose poncha, served in the bars of Câmara de Lobos. It combines aguardente de cana (a spirit distilled from sugarcane juice), honey, and lemon or orange juice. It’s stirred with a wooden stick called a mexelote. It’s strong: let someone else drive, or save it for the evening in Funchal.

practical_info.tip: Drink poncha in small quantities: ask for it without sugar if you prefer it less sweet.

visits.text: The family of Zarco, the navigator who claimed Madeira for Portugal, had their second home at Quinta das Cruzes in Funchal. Converted into a museum in 1953, the house displays 17th-century Portuguese furniture carved from exotic woods imported mainly from Brazil. It also holds Chinese porcelain from the Qing dynasty, China’s last imperial dynasty. Allow 1 hour, including the garden; open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

activities.text: You’ll return the car at Madeira Airport in Santa Cruz, about 20 minutes from Funchal via the expressway. Arrive early and monitor your flight’s status: wind often restricts air traffic at this airport. If you have time before boarding, Machico’s light-sand beach is a few minutes’ drive away.

practical_info.tip: Fill up the tank before returning the car if your rental agreement requires it.

seo.h1_title: Madeira in 7 Days: Funchal, Levadas, and Pico Ruivo
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7-day driving itinerary circles Madeira from Funchal, with overnight stays in Santana, Porto Moniz, and Calheta. It alternates hikes on designated trails (Pico do Areeiro, Pico Ruivo, Ponta de São Lourenço, 25 Fontes) with gardens, museums, and swims in lava pools. Trails must be booked through the SIMplifica portal, and nonresidents must pay a fee.
seo.seo_hook: Madeira in 7 days: Funchal’s old town, Monte toboggans, the Pico Ruivo trail, the 25 Fontes levada, and Porto Moniz’s lava pools.
featured_list: Funchal: Sé Cathedral with its cedar ceiling, a market dating to 1940, and Madeira wine cellars
Monte: cable car, tropical garden, and wicker toboggans since 1850
Pico do Areeiro: the island’s third-highest peak at 1,818 m, accessible by car
Pico Ruivo: Madeira’s highest point at 1,862 m via PR1.2
Ponta de São Lourenço: 4 km of trail on a volcanic peninsula
Fanal: til trees, a species of laurel, more than a century old in the Laurissilva, Madeira’s laurel forest
Porto Moniz: natural lava pools and an aquarium in a fort dating to 1730
Cabo Girão: glass platform 580 m above the sea

places_taglines.PT::machico: Bay where Zarco landed in 1419, with a beach made of Sahara sand.

places_taglines.PT::pico-do-areeiro: Madeira’s third-highest peak at 1,818 m, accessible by road.
places_taglines.PT::pico-ruivo: Madeira’s highest point at 1,862 m, with a mountain hut.
places_taglines.PT::sao-vicente: Town on the north coast with a chapel built into a rock.
places_taglines.PT::seixal: Black sand beach and terraced vineyards on the north coast.
places_taglines.PT::porto-moniz: Natural lava pools and an aquarium housed in a fort dating from 1730.
places_taglines.PT::fanal: Forest of Madeira laurels well over a century old, in Madeira’s Laurissilva.
places_taglines.PT::rabacal: Starting point for the 25 Fontes and Risco levadas, in the Laurissilva.
places_taglines.PT::calheta: Contemporary art museum, sugarcane mill, and sandy beach in the west.

Monte: a ride downhill in carros de cesto, wicker sleds in use since 1850
Pico Ruivo: Madeira’s highest point at 1,862 m, via PR1.2
Rabaçal: 25 springs at the end of the Levada das 25 Fontes

itineraries.title: Minho in 6 Days: Guimarães, Braga, Ponte de Lima, Caminha
itineraries.subtitle: In 6 days, travel from Guimarães and Braga to the ramparts of Valença and the mouth of the Minho River at Caminha.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday: you will be in Barcelos on Thursday, market day, and museums that close on Mondays will be open. At Guimarães Castle, only the inner courtyard is open to visitors while the ramparts are being restored.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs in Braga of 21 °C in May and 28 °C in July and August. Avoid October through January, the rainiest months, with nearly 200 mm of rain per month. Even in May, bring a raincoat: more than 100 mm of rain still falls that month.
specialties: Voies vertes au bord du Minho

activities.text: You will land at Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport, north of Porto, or arrive by train at São Bento Station, right in the city center. This is the starting point for your loop through Minho, the region in northwestern Portugal separated from Spain by the Minho River. Pick up your rental car when you arrive. Guimarães, your first stop, is 53 km from the airport, about a 40-minute drive.

map_keywords: Paço dos Duques de Bragança Guimarães

visits.text: Medieval in appearance, yet rebuilt in the 20th century: that is the paradox of the Paço dos Duques de Bragança, the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza. Afonso, Count of Barcelos and later the first Duke of Braganza, began having it built in the 1420s. The dukes later moved to Vila Viçosa, and the palace became a barracks in 1807. It was rebuilt from 1937 to 1959 under the Estado Novo, the authoritarian regime of the time. This highly interpretive restoration remains controversial. The palace is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.: admission is €10, or €13 including the castle.

According to tradition, Afonso Henriques, Portugal’s first king, was born at Castelo de Guimarães, the castle crowning the hill above the city. Countess Mumadona Dias had the first tower built here in the 10th century to protect a monastery. Right next door, the small Church of São Miguel do Castelo preserves the baptismal font where the future king is said to have been baptized. During the ongoing restoration, only the inner courtyard is open to visitors: the wall walk and keep are closed. Admission is €5.

Houses with granite ground floors and wooden upper stories, an olive tree amid the cobblestones: this is Largo da Oliveira, the heart of the historic center designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. According to tradition, a withered olive tree here turned green again in 1342, three days after a cross was placed beside it. The neighboring church took its name from the tree: Nossa Senhora da Oliveira, Our Lady of the Olive Tree. In front stands the Padrão do Salado, a small monument dating from 1340 that commemorates the Battle of Salado, won that year by King Afonso IV, who had come to Castile’s aid. Return in the evening, when the outdoor cafés come alive.

One object in particular makes a visit to the Museu de Alberto Sampaio worthwhile: King João I’s gambeson. This padded garment was worn beneath armor. The king wore it at the Battle of Aljubarrota on August 14, 1385, a victory that helped secure Portugal’s independence. He later offered it to the Virgin of Guimarães. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. A combined ticket with the Palace of the Dukes and the castle costs €17.

“Aqui nasceu Portugal,” meaning “Portugal was born here,” appears in large letters on the Torre da Alfândega, a tower in Guimarães’s old city walls. It recalls the Battle of São Mamede, fought near the city on June 24, 1128. That day, Afonso Henriques defeated the troops of his own mother, Countess Teresa. This victory is presented as the birth of the country. Step back a little to take your photo.

Leather was still being worked in the Zona de Couros, the old tanners’ district south of the old town, as recently as 2005. Hides soaked in vats, then in a bath of tannin extracted from oak bark: this substance turns hides into leather. Since 2023, the district has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Walk among the old vats and the tall brick chimney, between the Alameda gardens and the train station.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, head up Mount Penha on the Teleférico de Guimarães, the cable car linking the city to the summit. The cabin travels nearly 1.7 km and climbs 366 m in less than eight minutes. At the top, at 617 m, enormous fallen granite boulders form small caves, one of which has become a chapel. The Penha sanctuary, in the center of the park, was inaugurated in 1947. Hours vary by season, and the cable car stops running in bad weather: check turipenha.pt before setting out.

practical_info.tip: Reduced winter hours and possible closures in bad weather: check turipenha.pt the day before.

visits.text: Portugal did not yet exist when Sé de Braga, the cathedral, was consecrated in 1089: the region was then part of the Kingdom of León. It is Portugal’s first cathedral. Count Henry and Countess Teresa, the parents of Afonso Henriques, are buried in the Chapel of the Kings. Go up to the coro alto, the choir loft, for a close look at the two gilded wooden organs from the 1730s. A ticket covering the cathedral, choir loft, and treasury costs about €5. Avoid Sunday mornings, which are reserved for Mass.

Boxwood trimmed into geometric patterns, sculpted cedars, and ruined stone arcades: the Jardim de Santa Bárbara runs alongside the east wing of Braga’s former archbishops’ palace. These arches are the remains of a palace wing destroyed by fire in 1866. The garden itself was only laid out in 1955, around a fountain topped with a statue of Saint Barbara. Admission is free. Allow 15 minutes, then head to Largo do Paço, the palace square, right next door.

Walk beneath the Arco da Porta Nova to enter Braga’s old town. This city gate was opened in 1512. The Baroque and Neoclassical arch visible today is attributed to André Soares, an 18th-century architect from Braga. He also designed the Church of Lapa, which you will see in Arcos de Valdevez. From the gate, continue on foot toward the cathedral.

The Palácio do Raio is more than 250 years old and has a facade covered in blue azulejos, the painted ceramic tiles typical of Portugal. This 18th-century Baroque and Rococo palace now houses an exhibition space devoted to the history of the Misericórdia, a charitable brotherhood in Braga. View the facade from the sidewalk across the street: it offers the best view of the decoration as a whole.

More than 570 zigzagging steps lead up to the Church of Bom Jesus do Monte, a sanctuary designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, about 6 km from central Braga. The stairway forms a Way of the Cross, with chapels depicting the Passion of Christ. On the Stairway of the Five Senses, each landing has its own fountain, one for each sense, from sight to taste. The Neoclassical church at the top, begun in 1784, is the work of architect Carlos Amarante. Walk up early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, and take the funicular back down.

For the widest view over Braga, head up to the Santuário do Sameiro, less than 2 km from Bom Jesus. Construction of this sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin began in 1863. A grand staircase of 265 steps leads to the basilica. The best viewpoint is at the top of its dome, overlooking the city and the Minho Valley. Come in the late afternoon for softer light.

activities.text: Braga’s most surprising ride lasts three minutes: the Elevador do Bom Jesus, the sanctuary’s funicular, which has been operating since 1882. It runs without electricity, powered by the weight of water. At the top, the tank of the car about to descend is filled with water. Now heavier, it descends and pulls the other car uphill, after that car’s tank has been emptied at the bottom. It is the world’s oldest water-counterbalanced funicular still in operation. In summer, it departs every half hour, at 25 and 55 minutes past the hour, from 8:55 a.m. to 7:55 p.m.

practical_info.tip: In winter, the funicular stops for an hour at noon and closes around 6 p.m.

activities.text: You can take a breather in Bom Jesus Park, with around 26 hectares of woodland and gardens at the top of the hill. You’ll find viewpoints, an artificial grotto designed by Swiss architect Ernest Korrodi, and a small lake with rowboats for rent. The shaded paths are pleasant during the hot hours of summer. Bring a picnic so you can enjoy the setting at your own pace.

visits.text: A roasted rooster that crows to save an innocent man: that is the legend behind the Cruzeiro do Senhor do Galo, an 18th-century stone cross. According to the story, a Galician pilgrim on his way to Santiago de Compostela was wrongly condemned. To prove his innocence, he declared that the roasted rooster served to the judge would crow. The rooster crowed, and the man was saved. The cross is displayed in the ruins of the Paço dos Condes de Barcelos, a free open-air museum. Work on this palace began in the 15th century under Count Afonso, who also built the palace in Guimarães.

The Ponte Medieval de Barcelos, a Gothic bridge over the Cávado, was built between 1325 and 1328 on the orders of Count Pedro Afonso. Its five unequal arches connect the town to the suburb of Barcelinhos on the opposite bank. Pilgrims on the Portuguese Way to Santiago still cross it today. Right beside the palace ruins, the Igreja Matriz, the main church, combines Romanesque and Gothic architecture. Cross the bridge for the view of town, then head back up to the church.

In December 1504, according to tradition, a cross outlined in black earth appeared on the ground at Campo da Feira. To shelter it, Barcelos built the Igreja do Senhor Bom Jesus da Cruz, a Baroque church dating to 1710 and decorated with azulejo tile panels. Every May 3, the Festa das Cruzes, the Festival of the Crosses, draws crowds here. The church borders the market square: visit on a Thursday between browsing the stalls at the fair.

You’ll get a sweeping view of Barcelos from the top of the Torre de Porta Nova, a 15th-century tower. It is the only one of the five gates in the old town wall still standing. It houses the tourist office and a permanent exhibition of local crafts. Admission is free. On weekdays, the tower is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The Museu de Olaria, the pottery museum, is worth a visit even if you don’t collect anything. Opened in 1963, it brings together nearly 10,000 pottery objects from Portugal and Portuguese-speaking countries. Barcelos is known for its figurado, humorous clay figurines with exaggerated features depicting farmers, musicians, and Nativity figures. This craftsmanship has earned it UNESCO Creative City status for Crafts and Folk Art. Admission to the museum is free.

activities.text: Live animals, wicker baskets, cured meats, and piles of clothing: every Thursday, the Feira de Barcelos fills Campo da República, which locals also call Campo da Feira. Its origins date back to the 15th century. You’ll find fruits and vegetables, pastries, shoes, and crafts from Minho: basketry, tinware, embroidery, and woodwork. Come in the morning and keep some change handy for small purchases.

practical_info.tip: The market is held only on Thursdays: plan your trip so you’re in Barcelos that day.

map_keywords: Museu dos Terceiros Ponte de Lima
Avenida dos Plátanos Ponte de Lima

visits.text: Roman on one side, Gothic on the other: the bridge that gave Ponte de Lima its name combines two eras. Roman arches survive near the right bank; the rest dates to the 14th century. Statues of Roman soldiers on the riverbank recall a legend. In the 2nd century BCE, the troops of General Decimus Junius Brutus refused to cross the Lima. They mistook it for the Lethe, the river that erases memory in Greek mythology. The general crossed and called each soldier by name from the opposite bank. The bridge is for pedestrians only.

Shaded by plane trees, Avenida dos Plátanos, nicknamed “the street of fantasy,” is the promenade in central Ponte de Lima. The town received its charter from Countess Teresa in 1125 and is considered Portugal’s oldest vila. Vila is an official Portuguese designation between a village and a city. Largo de Camões, at the entrance to the bridge, is laid out around a fountain, the Chafariz Nobre. Every other Monday, the town’s large market, one of the oldest in the country, sets up on the riverbank.

Plaques attached to the Torre da Cadeia Velha show how high the Lima’s major floods reached. This tower is one of two surviving towers from the ramparts, built between 1359 and around 1370. It now houses the town’s tourist information center: ask for a map here. Nearby, the Igreja Matriz, the main church, was built by local residents starting in 1425. Take a look at its Gothic portal.

For sacred art, the Museu dos Terceiros is the best place to visit in Ponte de Lima. It occupies two neighboring churches: Santo António dos Frades and the church of the Ordem Terceira, a lay confraternity. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. It is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Walk along the Ecovia do Lima, the greenway that follows the river for around 70 km. A greenway is a path reserved for pedestrians and cyclists. From Ponte de Lima, a frequently recommended section heads upstream to Ponte da Barca, 15 km away. Take a 1-hour round-trip walk along the water, or rent a bike in town to go farther.

In Ponte de Lima, arroz de sarrabulho is nicknamed the “black gold” of local cuisine. The full version of this pork and rice dish comes with rojões, chunks of fried pork, and tripas enfarinhadas, tripe coated in flour and then fried. Pair it with vinho verde, the regional wine, made here from the Loureiro grape variety. Save it for dinner: it’s a hearty dish.

map_keywords: Igreja da Lapa Arcos de Valdevez
Paço da Giela Arcos de Valdevez

visits.text: Oval on the outside and octagonal on the inside, the Igreja da Lapa in Arcos de Valdevez plays with shapes. Completed in 1767, it is attributed to André Soares, the architect of Braga’s Arco da Porta Nova. Beneath its lofty dome, look at the Rococo altarpieces, the large carved wooden panels behind the altars, and the ornate grilles. Step inside if the door is open: 15 minutes is enough.

The Paço da Giela, a national monument on the outskirts of Arcos de Valdevez, combines a 14th-century tower with 16th-century living quarters. Its windows are Manueline, a Portuguese decorative style from the early 16th century. An earlier fortification already stood on the site in the 11th century. The rooms display objects found during excavations and trace the building’s development. Opening hours vary by season: check with the tourist office before visiting.

activities.text: In 1140, on the banks of the Vez, Afonso Henriques and King Alfonso VII of Castile faced each other in a tournament, a contest between knights governed by rules, rather than a pitched battle. This Recontro de Valdevez is seen as a step toward Portugal’s independence. Spend 30 minutes strolling along the banks of the Vez. Farther upstream, the Ecovia do Vez, a 32 km greenway, follows the river to the village of Sistelo. Before leaving, try rebuçados dos Arcos, large local candies.

visits.text: Monção’s ramparts are bastioned fortifications, with pointed projections that allowed defenders to fire along the walls. Construction began in 1656, following a design by French engineer Miguel de L’École, whose work you’ll see again in Valença. Besieged by the Spanish from October 1658 to February 1659, the fortified town eventually surrendered. Two of its five gates remain, including the Porta de Salvaterra. From the riverside ramparts, look across to Salvaterra de Miño, the Spanish town on the opposite bank.

In 1369, according to the accounts, the Castilians besieged Monção, and the town was starving. Deu-la-Deu Martins, wife of the alcaide, the castle governor, baked bread with the last of the flour. She threw it to the besiegers as though the storerooms were full. Discouraged, they lifted the siege. Praça Deu-la-Deu bears her name, and Monção’s coat of arms shows a woman holding a loaf of bread in each hand. Her tomb is in the Igreja Matriz, a 13th-century Romanesque church.

Before tasting, it helps to understand: that is the role of the Museu do Alvarinho, housed in the Casa do Curro on Praça Deu-la-Deu. This municipal museum presents Monção and Melgaço as the birthplace of Alvarinho, the grape variety behind the region’s reputation. It also explores the area’s landscapes, traditions, and historic houses. Allow 30 minutes; opening hours are published on the municipal website.

activities.text: Book a guided tour of the Palácio da Brejoeira, 5 km south of Monção: tours start at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. and last around 1 hour 30 minutes. Work on this Neoclassical palace began around 1806 and took nearly thirty years. Its estate includes 18 hectares of Alvarinho vineyards, and its first wine went on sale in 1976. In 2025, the “Património” package (interior, gardens, chapel, and old wine cellar) cost €9.50. Add a tasting for €3 to €5.50.

practical_info.tip: Guided tours at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.: arrive a little early.

visits.text: More than 5 km of walls surround the Fortaleza de Valença, which guarded the Spanish border. It has two defensive enclosures, or sets of ramparts: the Magistral, the older of the two, and the Coroada, linked by the Porta do Meio. Construction began in 1641, during the war that restored Portugal’s independence from Spain. Work was completed in 1713. In 1809, Napoleon’s troops blew up the Porta do Sol. Park in the Coroada, to the south, then climb to the Baluarte do Socorro, the bastion with the best view of Tui.

The Igreja de Santo Estêvão, Neoclassical but Romanesque in origin, has a 1st-century milestone in its forecourt. This stone column marked distances along Roman road XIX, the road from Braga. Inside, a niche to the right of the altar holds a Virgin nursing the Child, a rare image in Portuguese religious art. Continue to the Igreja de Santa Maria dos Anjos, Valença’s main parish church, on a charming square in the old town.

activities.text: If you walk across the Ponte Internacional to Tui, Spain, set your watch forward one hour. Spain uses Central European Time, one hour ahead of Portugal. Built in 1886, this 384 m bridge carries trains on its upper level and road traffic below. Its lattice structure of intersecting iron beams recalls Gustave Eiffel’s style. Tui’s old town and fortress cathedral are about a 1.5 km walk away.

Allow 2 hours for the Ecopista do Rio Minho, the greenway along the former railroad between Valença and Monção. Opened in 2004, it was the country’s first greenway built on an abandoned rail line. In 2017, it placed third in the European Greenways Awards. It starts at Valença station and follows the river for 15 km through dense woods. Take an out-and-back walk; if you prefer cycling, ask the tourist office near the Porta do Sol where to rent a bike.

The cannons remain on the ramparts, but Valença now lives on trade. The fortress streets are lined with stores selling household linens, very popular with Spanish shoppers. On weekends, crowds fill the narrow streets. Shop early in the morning or late in the day, when the old town becomes quiet again.

map_keywords: Castelo de Vila Nova de Cerveira
Aquamuseu do Rio Minho Vila Nova de Cerveira
Miradouro do Cervo Vila Nova de Cerveira

visits.text: Eight rectangular towers and an oval defensive enclosure beside the river: the Castelo de Vila Nova de Cerveira faces Galicia. The town received its charter from King Dom Dinis in 1321. Reinforced against Spain in the 17th century, the fortress prevented Napoleon’s troops from crossing the Minho in 1809. Above the old gate, the Nossa Senhora da Ajuda chapel dates from 1650. Walk around the walls for views of the river.

According to local legend, a “Cervo Rei,” or stag king, gave the lands of Cerveira their name. Sculptor José Rodrigues dedicated a large stag statue to him, set at an elevation of about 300 m on Alto do Castro, in the Serra da Gávea, the mountain overlooking the town. It can be seen from more than 10 km away. Head up late in the day for views of the town, the Minho River, and Spain.

Since 1978, Vila Nova de Cerveira has hosted the Bienal de Cerveira, an international contemporary art exhibition held every two years. Its organizer, the Fundação Bienal de Cerveira, lists current exhibitions on its website. Check it before you come to find out what will be open during your visit.

activities.text: You can see otters up close at the Aquamuseu do Rio Minho, in Castelinho Park beside the river. This municipal museum combines an aquarium, an otter enclosure, and a fishing museum. Admission costs €2. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October, closing at 5 p.m. in winter. It is closed on Mondays.

visits.text: Outdoor café seating surrounds a fountain dating from 1551: the Praça do Conselheiro Silva Torres is the heart of Caminha. This Renaissance fountain, the chafariz, stands at its center. The Torre do Relógio, or clock tower, is a former keep in the ramparts. Around the square, see the 16th-century Igreja da Misericórdia and Casa Pita, a Neo-Manueline residence that imitates early 16th-century Portuguese decoration. The tourist office is on nearby Rua Direita, a cobblestone street with ornate balconies.

The finest detail of the Igreja Matriz de Caminha is above your head. Its coffered ceiling, made of recessed chestnut-wood panels, is attributed to Francisco Muñoz. Its decoration shows Mudéjar influence, meaning it was inspired by the art of Spain’s Muslims. Begun in 1488 by Basque builders and completed in 1556, the church blends Gothic, Manueline, and Renaissance styles. Spanish troops bombarded it in the 17th century during the Restoration War between Portugal and Spain. Look up as soon as you enter.

activities.text: Head to Foz do Minho, the river’s mouth, then to Praia de Moledo, a beach of white sand and rocks 4 km southwest of the center. Offshore, on an islet, the Forte da Ínsua occupies the site of a 14th-century Franciscan friary; King Manuel I had it rebuilt. Opposite, on the Spanish side, Mount Santa Tecla rises to 341 m. The beach attracts surfers and windsurfers: bring a windbreaker.

If you prefer walking, the Ecovia do Cristelo links Caminha to Moledo over 1.5 km. The Ecovia de la Foz do Minho follows the river’s mouth for about 1 km. These short paths for pedestrians and cyclists extend the greenway that follows the river upstream toward Vila Nova de Cerveira and Valença. Allow 45 minutes for each round-trip walk, including photo stops.

Porto is about 90 km from Caminha, a little over an hour’s drive south. Return your car at Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport, north of the city, if you are flying out. If you are staying in Porto for a few days, return it as soon as you arrive in the city, near São Bento station.

seo.h1_title: Minho in 6 Days: Guimarães, Braga, Ponte de Lima, Caminha
seo.intro_paragraph: This 6-day road trip starts in Porto and explores Minho in northwestern Portugal. It begins with Guimarães and Braga, then heads to Barcelos on market day and Ponte de Lima. It then follows the Minho River, which forms the border with Spain, from Monção to Caminha via Valença and Vila Nova de Cerveira.
seo.seo_hook: The palace in Guimarães, Bom Jesus in Braga, the Thursday market in Barcelos, and the fortress in Valença: explore Minho in 6 days starting from Porto.
featured_list: Guimarães: the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza, begun around 1420 and restored from 1937 to 1959
Braga: Bom Jesus do Monte, more than 570 steps and a water-powered funicular dating from 1882
Barcelos: the Thursday market and the legend of the rooster
Ponte de Lima: a Roman and Gothic bridge completed around 1370
Valença: more than 5 km of walls facing Spain

itineraries.title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro
itineraries.subtitle: Explore Ribeira, the Gaia wine cellars, Clérigos Tower, and Foz over 2 days on foot, by tram, and by cable car.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Saturday: Bolhão Market is closed on Sundays and public holidays. Buy your Livraria Lello ticket in advance—it is required for entry—and book your wine cellar tour during peak season.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with highs of 20 to 26 °C and very little rain in July and August. If possible, avoid October through January, the rainiest months, with more than 120 mm of rain per month. Winters remain mild, with temperatures between 6 and 17 °C: bring a raincoat and good shoes for the hilly streets.

visits.text: Blue and white from the sidewalk to the roof: Capela das Almas, on Rua de Santa Catarina, is entirely covered in azulejos, the painted ceramic tiles typical of Portugal. There are 15,947 of them. They tell the stories of Saint Francis of Assisi and Saint Catherine. Designed by Eduardo Leite, this decoration dates to 1929: before then, the walls were simply plastered and painted white. Cross the street to take in the entire side wall at a glance. The chapel interior is only open at certain times.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walking route of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

activities.text: Start your shopping at Mercado do Bolhão, the large covered market in central Porto. The building dates to 1914. It reopened on September 15, 2022, after more than four years of restoration. On the ground floor, stalls sell fish, meat, vegetables, and flowers. Upstairs, around ten restaurants offer a place to have lunch. Come on a Saturday morning: the market opens at 8 a.m. and is closed on Sundays.

practical_info.tip: Open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Saturday from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on public holidays. Bolhão metro station connects directly to the market.

visits.text: Avenida dos Aliados is the grand avenue in central Porto, laid out beginning in 1916. Its name honors the Allied countries of World War I. At the top stands Porto City Hall, the Paços do Concelho. Along one side, the former Café Imperial now houses a McDonald’s that humor website 9GAG dubbed “the most beautiful in the world.” Continue down the avenue to Liberty Square: São Bento station is just a two-minute walk away.

Few train stations are worth a detour without a train ticket: São Bento station is one of them. Its entrance hall is covered with around 20,000 azulejos, painted by Jorge Colaço between 1905 and 1916. The large blue panels depict Portuguese history, including the arrival on horseback of King John I and his English wife, Philippa of Lancaster, in Porto in 1387. A colorful frieze also shows the country’s past modes of transportation. The hall is still part of a working station: admire the walls while leaving room for travelers to pass.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walking route of 0.6 km in 10 minutes is correct.

visits.text: In 1387, King John I married the English princess Philippa of Lancaster in Sé do Porto, the city’s cathedral. They are the couple you just saw on horseback on the azulejos at São Bento. With its two square towers and battlements, the building resembles a fortified church. In the Gothic cloister, azulejos installed between 1729 and 1731 illustrate the Song of Songs, a love poem from the Bible. There is an admission fee for the cloister. The cathedral opens daily at 9 a.m.

activities.text: Cross Luís I Bridge on its upper deck: this bridge has two levels, and the upper one sits more than 45 m above the Douro. This metal bridge was inaugurated on October 31, 1886. It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, a former partner of Gustave Eiffel. Until 1944, pedestrians paid a toll of five réis, the former Portuguese currency, to cross from one bank to the other. Today, pedestrians share the upper deck with metro Line D: watch for approaching trains.

practical_info.tip: If you are afraid of heights, cross on the lower deck instead, close to the water; it is also open to pedestrians.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walking route of 0.4 km in 7 minutes is correct.

map_keywords: Mosteiro da Serra do Pilar Vila Nova de Gaia
Jardim do Morro Vila Nova de Gaia

visits.text: If you could keep just one view of Porto, choose the one from the terrace of Serra do Pilar Monastery, on the Vila Nova de Gaia bank. Across the river, Ribeira, the cathedral, and Luís I Bridge rise in tiers above the water. The monastery’s distinctive feature is that both its church and its cloister are round. In 1809, the future Duke of Wellington, a British general, used it as a base to retake Porto from the French. Just below, Jardim do Morro, a terraced garden, slopes down toward the river: return at sunset.

to_next_leg.road_type: Gaia cable car down to the quay, about 4 minutes

map_keywords: Caves Sandeman Vila Nova de Gaia
Caves Taylor's Vila Nova de Gaia

activities.text: Port wine takes its name from the city, but it ages across the river in the Vila Nova de Gaia wine cellars. In 1777, Gaia became the official wine storage location for all exporters. Port is a fortified wine: grape brandy is added to stop fermentation and preserve the fruit’s sugar. At Sandeman, on the quay, the short tour lasts 50 minutes and includes three ports (€23). At Taylor’s, on Rua do Choupelo, you explore independently with an audio guide on your phone: bring your headphones.

practical_info.tip: Sandeman: daily from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and 2 p.m. to 6 p.m., with the last tours at 12:15 p.m. and 5:15 p.m. Taylor’s: cellars open daily from 10 a.m. to 6:15 p.m.; online reservations recommended.

to_next_leg.road_type: Crossing via the lower deck of Luís I Bridge
to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 1 km in 15 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: Arcades, cafés, and terraces right by the water: Ribeira is one of Porto’s oldest neighborhoods. The arcaded houses on Ribeira Square were rebuilt after a major fire in 1491. On the quay, a small memorial, the Alminhas da Ponte, commemorates the tragedy of 1809. That year, during the invasion by Napoleon’s troops, a bridge made of boats tied together collapsed, and many residents drowned. Save this neighborhood for late in the day, when the evening light bathes Luís I Bridge in gold.

It is called the Casa Escondida, the “hidden house”: a house barely more than a meter and a half wide, wedged between Carmo Church and the Carmelites Church. According to tradition, it separated the two churches so their religious communities would not live under the same roof. The Igreja do Carmo, built between 1756 and 1768, is recognizable by the large azulejo panel covering its side wall, installed in 1912. It depicts the founding of the Carmelite religious order. View it from the street. You can visit the hidden house with a ticket costing a few euros.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: Book a time slot before stepping into Livraria Lello: admission requires a ticket, priced at €15.95 on the official website. Opened in 1906, the bookstore owes its fame to its staircase. It looks like carved wood, but it is one of Portugal’s first concrete staircases, painted to imitate wood. Its red color resulted from a painting mistake during the 1993 restoration, and it was kept. The ticket price is deducted from the purchase of a book published by Lello. Suitcases and large backpacks are not allowed.

to_next_leg.justification: Walking route through central Porto: the routing engine calculated a driving detour along streets open to traffic; the current walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: The Torre dos Clérigos, or Clerics’ Tower, rises 75.6 m above central Porto. Designed by architect Nicolau Nasoni, it was completed in 1763. Nasoni asked to be buried in the crypt of the neighboring church, but no one knows exactly where his grave is. The 240 steps lead to the top, above the city’s rooftops. The €10 ticket includes the tower and museum. The site is open daily from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., with last admission 30 minutes before closing.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are a short walk apart in central Porto: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: In our opinion, the prettiest route down from São Bento to the river is Rua das Flores. Work on the street began in 1521 on the site of the bishop’s vegetable gardens, which were full of flowers—hence its name, “Street of Flowers.” Goldsmiths traditionally kept shops here, especially on the north side. Along the way, the Church of Mercy (Igreja da Misericórdia), begun in 1559, is worth a look. Take your time walking down to Largo de São Domingos, a small square near the Stock Exchange Palace.

to_next_leg.road_type: Descent to Largo de São Domingos

visits.text: In 1832, a fire destroyed the cloister of São Francisco Convent. On its ruins, Porto’s merchants began building the Palácio da Bolsa, or Stock Exchange Palace, in 1842. Beneath the glass dome of the Courtyard of Nations, painted coats of arms represent Portugal and its trading partners. The highlight of the visit is the Arab Room, inspired by the Alhambra, the palace of Granada’s Moorish kings. The guided tour lasts 30 minutes (€14). The group’s language, with French among the options, depends on the order of arrival.

to_next_leg.justification: The two sites are a short walk apart in central Porto: the routing engine returned a null value; the current walk of 0.1 km in 2 minutes is appropriate.

visits.text: Outside, a restrained Gothic church; inside, almost everything is gilded. The Igreja de São Francisco, or Church of Saint Francis, completed around 1425, was covered in carved and gilded wood during the 17th and 18th centuries, from the pillars to the ceiling. It is nicknamed the “golden church.” Look for the Tree of Jesse, a carved family tree commissioned in 1718: it depicts Jesus’s ancestors, including twelve kings of Judah. The ticket (€9) also includes admission to the catacombs, where monks lie buried beneath the floor. When you leave, tram 1 departs right next door from the Infante stop.

to_next_leg.road_type: Tram 1 along the Douro, from Infante to Passeio Alegre

visits.text: If the old tram 1 has rattled you around for a good half hour along the Douro, Jardim do Passeio Alegre is the place to catch your breath. This garden in Foz do Douro, the neighborhood at the river’s mouth, was designed by landscape architect Émile David. It features two 18th-century obelisks by Nicolau Nasoni, the architect of Clérigos Tower. A fountain designated a national monument completes the setting. Tram 1 terminates here: check the last departure time before strolling around, as service is reduced in winter.

activities.text: Walk to the end of the Molhe de Felgueiras, the breakwater built at the mouth of the Douro. Here, the river completes an 897 km journey that began in Spain and meets the Atlantic Ocean. The small, hexagonal, 10 m lighthouse, Farolim de Felgueiras, dates from 1886. Its light has been inactive since 2009, and it now retains only an audible signal for boats. Then walk along Avenida Dom Carlos I, facing the waves. In rough seas, stay well away from the end of the breakwater, which is exposed to waves.

practical_info.tip: To return to the center, take tram 1 from Passeio Alegre, or bus 500, which follows roughly the same route to Liberty Square (Praça da Liberdade).

seo.h1_title: Porto in 2 Days: Ribeira, Gaia Wine Cellars, and Foz do Douro
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Porto requires no car: explore the historic center, listed by UNESCO in 1996, on foot, ride the cable car in Vila Nova de Gaia, and take the tram to the ocean. The first day takes you from Bolhão Market to the port wine cellars, then to Ribeira. The second includes Livraria Lello, Clérigos Tower, and the Stock Exchange Palace before heading to Foz do Douro.
seo.seo_hook: Porto in 2 days: São Bento’s azulejos, the cathedral, port wine cellars in Gaia, Livraria Lello, Clérigos Tower, and tram 1 to the ocean.
featured_list: São Bento station: around 20,000 azulejos tell the story of Portugal
Luís I Bridge: two levels above the Douro since 1886
Vila Nova de Gaia: port wine cellars open for tours and tastings
Livraria Lello: a bookstore dating from 1906, with the admission ticket price credited toward a book
Clérigos Tower: 240 steps to the top
Stock Exchange Palace: an Arabian Hall inspired by the Alhambra
Foz do Douro: tram 1 and an 1886 lighthouse at the river’s mouth
